speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: MR. BALCER    PROTEST AGAINST THE ATTITUDE OF MR. HUMPHRYS  REQUEST FOR RETRACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. After the luncheon recess yesterday, the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) rose on a question of privilege and, quoting an extract from Le Droit of May 6 with reference to a questionnaire sent from the Ottawa district office, taxation division, Department of National Revenue, signed by F. A. Humphrys, assessment branch, the hon. member protested against the unworthy and anti-national attitude of a civil servant and asked for his dismissal.
I was not in the house at the time. Had I been here, I would have immediately protested against this unwarranted attack on a civil servant who was not here to defend himself. I have known Mr. Humphrys for the past eight or nine years, and have always found him a conscientious and efficient officer. In an interview yesterday afternoon with Mr. Humphrys, in the presence of the assistant deputy minister of the taxation division, Mr. Humphrys absolutely denied
having made the statement or reply attributed to him. Personally, I accept Mr. Humphrys' word.
Within the next few days, the estimates of the Department of National Revenue will be under review, and the house will have an opportunity to more fully discuss this and related matters. I shall be prepared to answer any questions and give all available information.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: STATEMENT AS TO POSITION IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a further short statement in regard to the grain position in Canada. In doing so I would first like to comment that during the past and present crop years we have been dealing with physical grain handling problems arising from abundant harvests. In
1951,	the western wheat crop was estimated at 529 million bushels, and this was followed by a crop of 664 million bushels in 1952, or a total wheat production of 1,193 million bushels from the two harvests. The production of oats in 1951 was 340 million bushels and in 1952, 346 million bushels, or 686 million bushels in the two years.
In the case of barley, 1951 production was 234 million bushels and 1952 production was 281 million bushels, or a combined barley production of 515 million bushels in 1951 and
1952.
In all the history of the west never have these quantities of grain been harvested in two successive years.
The phenomenal grain production in the prairie provinces in the last two years has been accompanied by an excellent demand. The extent of overseas demand for grain is indicated by the fact that in 1951-52, total grain exports-including wheat flour-from Canada amounted to 506 million bushels, an all-time record; and during the present crop year exports are running substantially ahead of the volume of a year ago. Our exports for the crop year 1952-53 should exceed the record levels of the last crop year by a substantial margin.
With this background I would now like to give the house an estimate of delivery possibilities in the prairie provinces for the balance of the crop year.

Grain
First of all, I would like to observe that producers' deliveries of grain up to April 30 amounted to 573 million bushels. This is the largest delivery of grain ever recorded in the corresponding period of any crop year. When we consider that we started the crop year with not more than 125 million bushels of immediately available country elevator space, I think you will agree that we have had an excellent movement of grain out of country elevators this year and an excellent turnover of country elevator space. Producers will, of course, continue to deliver grain in substantial volume right up to the end of the crop year. I have requested the Canadian wheat board to provide me with its estimate of the delivery position for the balance of the crop year and I will summarize the board's appraisal of the position.
According to the latest estimate of elevator agents, producers had marketable surpluses from 1952 crop of all grains amounting to 964 million bushels. This figure is about 37 million bushels lower than our earlier estimate and, of course, could be affected by crop development over the next 90 days.
Based on the grain movement to date, and after allowing for an increase in country elevator storage capacity and more efficient use of both country and terminal storage this year as a result of the dry harvest, we believe it will be possible to provide for firm deliveries of about 830 million bushels by July 31, 1953. This will be an increase of about 110 million bushels over the quantities of grain delivered in 1951-52. Up to the present time producers' deliveries have amounted to about 573 million bushels and we have, therefore, to make space available for a further 257 million bushels to provide for total producers' marketings up to the objective of 830 million bushels.
We estimate . that about 830 million bushels of grain can be delivered under our basic quota of 15 bushels per seeded acre on wheat, oats and barley, and the supplementary three-bushel delivery quota on total wheat, oats and barley acreage. Therefore, it looks now as though this will be the limit of our delivery quotas for the present crop year, although, of course, we will keep the position in continuous review for the balance of the crop year.
On May 1 the supplementary three-bushel quota became effective at every delivery point in the west and two weeks later, on May 15 all delivery points become alternative points. This means that producers may deliver their grain up to the 18-bushel quota at any station in the west where space is available.
As closely as we can estimate, total deliveries of around 830 million bushels will allow about 532 million bushels of wheat, 150 million bushels of barley, 120 million bushels of oats, 18 million bushels of rye and 10 million bushels of flax to be delivered.
To accomplish this, space must be found for about 165 million bushels of wheat, 49 million bushels of oats, 35 million bushels of barley and about 8 million bushels of flaxseed and rye.
If the foregoing estimates prove to be substantially correct, we will have a farm carryover on July 31 of about 133 million bushels of grain. The farm carryover will be largely in areas with the highest yield per acre in 1952.

Doukhobor situation in Kootenays extremely critical. Unless some action taken immediately expect violence will break out. Strongly recommend that your government under the powers of the War Measures Act proclaim an immediate curfew on all Doukhobors in the Kootenay district of British Columbia.

The Hon. W. A. C. Bennett,
Premier of British Columbia,
Victoria, B.C.
Replying in absence of the Prime Minister to your telegram to him requesting curfew under War Measures Act directed against Doukhobors in Kootenays might I say that the action that you propose that we should take would constitute a clear invasion Of your own wide field of provincial responsibility for the administration of justice. What really is involved is the exercise of your own indisputable and wide authority under heading fourteen of section ninety-two of the British North America Act to administer justice and enforce law and order in the province of British Columbia. speechtext:
A couple of days ago the hon. member for Peterborough West raised a question in connection with June 2 next, the date of Her

Majesty's coronation. The situation is that a proclamation in connection with this matter was issued on the 22nd day of January last, under which June 2 next is proclaimed as a day of "general thanksgiving and rejoicing on the occasion of our coronation".
Under the Interpretation Act, chapter 1 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927:
In every act, unless the context otherwise requires, the word "holiday" includes . . . and any day appointed by proclamation for a general fast or thanksgiving.
I would judge that the interpretation therefore is that the 2nd day of June is a holiday.

But, as I say, we are in the midst of negotiations, and nothing could be said now to the advantage of anyone.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Do I understand the minister to say that there is no cause for dissatisfaction or concern on his part? Is there not a rumour current to the effect that Canadair is taking over the operation of the plant?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: No, that is wholly a misstatement. Mr. Notman, who happens to be the president of Canadair Limited, is also a member of the Canadian Arsenals Limited board. In his capacity as member of the Arsenals board he has been looking into production at Sorel for Canadian Arsenals and for myself. But no one has taken over Sorel Industries Limited. The management has not been changed in any particular.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Has the minister any information-if he has not, perhaps he could get it and give it to me, I would hope before the end of the discussion on these estimates, but if not, at a later time-as to how many of these guns that plant has produced, how
IMr. Fulton.1

many they have delivered in Canada, and the average cost per gun?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: No, I cannot give that information. In the first place, deliveries are being made under the United States contract, and, in the second place, information about deliveries of guns and ammunition is classified information which cannot be given publicly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not rise with the intention of taking any great length of time of the committee, but I have one or two questions to ask the minister.
On several occasions sessional returns have been brought down to the house. The hon. member for Eglinton and other hon. members have placed on the record details in connection with purchases of large quantities of small personal equipment. I would suggest that there might be a change in the purchasing policy of the department.
If my recollection is correct, there have been purchases of large quantities of shaving brushes-I believe something in the nature of 150,000. There have also been large purchases of tooth brushes, tooth paste and other items of a personal nature. Has the government given consideration to making an extra allowance to members of the forces so that they could look after the purchases of those items? My understanding is that in times of war-and I am thinking particularly of the first world war-nothing of that kind has been supplied to the armed forces. It was recognized that that was taken care of in their allowances. I am just wondering whether it would not save a lot of trouble, expense, administration and the making of contracts and so forth if the government would give a little extra to the armed forces to take care of these items. It would not amount to more than a few cents a day and then the forces could look after these things themselves. These miscellaneous items are mainly of a personal nature and I wonder if they could not be handled better in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I am unable to answer that question as the policy is determined by the Minister of National Defence. I suppose the hon. member is asking this question under the capital assistance item on the basis this would be capital assistance to the individuals of the troops. We are simply the purchasing agents; when we get a requisition we fill it. Whether or not the requisition is necessary is a matter for another department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
There was one question that I omitted to ask when we were dealing with Sorel Industries. It has been rumoured that the Americans are pulling out of that area,

selling their houses and so on. Can the minister give assurance that no dissatisfaction is being expressed by the United States which might form a basis for this rumour?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
I do not know where my hon. friend gets his gossip. I have heard nothing about any reduction in the contract. There are certain contracts covering the 3-inch 50-calibre guns and there are contracts covering other heavy artillery for the United States. As far as I know the	situation is unchanged. I know of
no house in Sorel owned by any American who has to do with the gun contract. Whether they are moving out or not, I do not know, but if they are it is to make way for someone else or because their inspection staff service is not required. My officers tell me that we are taking over more of the inspection now that production is getting to a stage where the United States feel that their inspection is not required to the extent it was in the early stages of production.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I have just one question to ask, and perhaps I might preface it by saying that I had intended to make a speech on this matter but I am prepared to let it go. I hold in my hand a document which the minister laid on the table of the house on April 12, 1945. This was a government white paper on employment and income with special reference to the initial period of reconstruction. Included in that very interesting white paper -that is the reason why my question is appropriate on this item-there is a reference to the conversion of government-owned plants and others which the government had in mind once world war II was over. My question is an obvious one. We do not know what the situation will be in the immediate future but the news from the Far East is encouraging and we dare to hope that there may soon be the possibility of tapering off the defence construction and the defence production programs. Has the government any plans or any white paper for that eventuality comparable to the plans and white paper that the minister tabled in April, 1945?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend has pretty well answered his own question. The preparedness program must extend for a considerable time. The only development so far has been the working out by the department of a program for the rental of tools and space in government-owned plants for civilian work when defence production drops below a level that will provide all of the employment of which the plant is capable. I think there has been one instance where that has happened. The rental includes the
Supply-Defence Production plant facilities and the use of machines which will be used on civilian work.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I point out to the minister that the item we are discussing is for $50 million less than it was a year ago. I suggest that I was not out of line in using the phrase "tapering off". I feel that in the light of that eventuality the government should go further than has been suggested by the answer the minister made just now and should indicate to the house and to the country what are its plans for the conversion of industry in order to maintain a high level of employment and a high standard of living if we are fortunate enough at an early date to enter a period when we can hope for peace.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: The reason this capital assistance is dropping off is that the facilities required for our program have pretty well been completed. I would not think that we will be required to build any new facilities after the current fiscal year. The dropping off of the capital assistance program does not mean that production is dropping off. As a matter of fact, production is coming up to its peak at the present time.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
81.	To provide for payment of grants to municipalities in lieu of taxes on crown-owned defence plants operated by private contractors, $400,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Can the
minister indicate how this works out from the point of view of the municipality? On what basis are these grants made? Could the minister indicate what the difference would be between the taxes .which a municipality would have got and the grant that is made in lieu of taxes when the Department of Defence Production takes over a plant and turns it into a crown-operated plant?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: The policy is to pay as a grant approximately the taxes that the firm would have paid had it been operated as a private plant.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
I hope the minister is quite sure that that is so. I want to put on the record the details of a case where it is felt that that is not what happened. This is referred to in a memorandum of the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities presented to the federal government at Ottawa on December 5, 1952. It would appear that the municipality concerned was surprised and taken aback when it found it was dealing with a government agency. After setting out the difficulties that the municipality was faced with, they go on to state, as reported on page 10, as follows:
The thinking of the municipal governments with respect to this matter is understandable. They are so severely dependent on property taxes for the

Supply-Defence Production major portion of their revenues that they view with concern the continuing and, in many cities, the mounting incidence of tax exempt federal crown property, a concern that becomes all the more serious when, as is so frequently the case, crown property is a significant percentage of the total real property in a municipality.
To add further to the grievance which the municipalities feel with respect to this matter is a recent interpretation of what constitutes crown property. We refer to the situation which has arisen in connection with the construction of the new industrial plants, privately managed, but being constructed with crown funds and ultimately to be bought by the. private management operating the plants from profits accruing as a result of their production on defence goods.
This new situation, of great significance to all Canadian municipalities, can best be illustrated by the developments that have recently taken place in Scarborough township, Ontario. In order to build up its revenues from industrial assessments, Scarborough township bought raw land and spent millions in providing essential services such as water, sewers, roads, etc. The intent of all this was to attract new taxpaying industry to the area. Some of this land was sold to two private companies, the John Inglis Company, Ltd., and the Lucas-Rotax Company, Ltd., both engaged in defence production. The sale was completed in good faith and at the time of sale it was understood that the land and plants thereon would be subject to the full municipal tax levy on the same basis as other industries and home owners in the township. It, therefore, came as a rude shock to the township council and the citizens of Scarborough to discover that this seemingly simple and straightforward transaction was not to yield the results expected.
When the township submitted its tax bills to the two companies it found that the properties in question had now been designated as crown property as the result of arrangements entered into between the companies concerned and the federal Department of Defence Production. Unknown to the municipal authorities, it now appears that the funds for the purchase qf land and construction of plants were actually provided by federal authorities with the understanding that the federal government will subsequently be reimbursed from the profits of defence production. In the meantime the property is vested in the name of a crown corporation under the terms of an agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Perhaps I could shorten this.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
There is
only one further paragraph that I want to read.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: It was written under a clear misapprehension.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
It was
apparently very widely shared. I will just read this and it will only take a moment. I want to get it on the record.
When the township of Scarborough protested the interpretation that these plants constituted crown property and, therefore, were exempt from municipal taxation, the matter was referred by the federal government to the Department of Justice, which gave its opinion "that these plants are not liable for taxation while owned by the crown and operated by the companies concerned exclusively on behalf of Her Majesty."
While it is true that the federal government has stated that it proposes to deal fairly with the

municipalities by making "grants in lieu of taxes" on these properties, on the basis of previous experience such grants are likely to amount to no more than 50 per cent of the normal tax assessment.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Well, the township corporation insisted that these were privately-owned plants. We said they were crown-owned plants, which they always were and which they always will be-or for a good time anyway.	We asked them to come here and
work out arrangements for grants in lieu of taxes. They did not come but they continued to try to prove that these were privately-owned plants. Finally I met the reeve at a function in Scarborough and I was able to convince him that they were publicly-owned plants.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
At what
point?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: And he did come to Ottawa and arrangements were worked out. In the case of the John Inglis Company the value of the lands and buildings-that is the amount for which they could be taxed-is $2,595,000. The normal tax as worked out by the assessment commissioner would be $68,840.40 and the grant in lieu of taxes for 1952 was $65,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Who worked that out?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I am sorry, that figure is for the coming year-1953-the first year of operation. For the Lucas-Rotax company the value of the land and buildings was set at $2,121,740 and the normal taxation according to the assessment commissioner would be $65,873.59. The agreed payment in lieu of taxes for 1953 will be approximately $60,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Who was the
assessment commissioner who fixed that?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I cannot tell you.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
It was the
commissioner for the federal government.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: No, it was the local assessment commissioner for the township of Scarborough.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Is the minister sure?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Then one
other question is this. When the sale was made, at what point did Defence Production emerge in this transaction?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
The Lucas-Rotax company
people bought the land on our behalf, at our request and with our consent. They were the purchasers.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
In their
name?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: It was immediately switched to our name. I am not sure whether it was in their name or in our name but the reason it was bought that way, as my hon. friend will quite understand, is that private enterprise can purchase to a little better advantage than the crown.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Yes, but I rather question a transaction where that is done-where the township sells in good faith with everybody knowing that what they wanted to have was ordinary taxation, but they wake up and find that they have not.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I would like to ask the minister another question. I notice that there is an increase in this item which indicates that there is an increase in the number of these crown-owned defence plants operated by private companies. I would like to ask the number of the plants and where they are situated.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: There are eleven plants. They are at North York, Etobicoke, Renfrew, Lachine, two at Scarborough, one in the township of Ross, the town of La Salle, the township of Toronto, and two in the parish of St. Laurent.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I was going to ask the minister a question in regard to last year's expenditures under this item. The details on page 158 indicate actual expenditure, by which, I take it, are meant grants to municipalities in lieu of taxes, to December 31, 1952. The sum of $175,500 is the actual amount to that date, and $49,500 is the amount estimated to be required for the balance of the fiscal year. The estimated total for 1952-53 is thus $225,000. Would the minister now give us the actual total, and would he put on Hansard, although it may be a long list, the municipalities to which payments were made and the amounts paid in each case?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Yes, I can do that for this year but I have not the expenditure detail for last year. The total was $214,842.36 and we have not got the detail here but we can easily get it for my hon. friend, and we will be glad to do so.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: That will show the amount paid to each municipality?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Yes, last year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
For the last fiscal year. I suppose there is a problem because the municipalities operate on a calendar year basis, but this statement is for the fiscal year commencing April 1. I understand that the grants were operative for the full fiscal year ended
Supply-Defence Production March 31, 1953, but what accounts for the increase from $213,000 to $400,000? Is there any change in the policy or is it simply a matter of more plants coming under the scope of grants in lieu of taxes?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Yes, Lucas-Rotax and several other plants operated for only a few months last year. There is no change in the policy followed and it is the same as for last year. There is, however, more property which has come on the tax rolls since that time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: As I recall it, the policy when announced applied to crown-owned property and also to property owned by crown corporations?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: May I ask if precisely the same policy is followed with respect to crown corporations on the one hand and crown-owned property on the other?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: It varies with the corporation. The corporation is subject to taxation-at least we have practically made it so. It is not legally subject to taxation because it is property of the crown. Nevertheless, the corporation works out its own tax deal with the taxing authority with which it is associated, and satisfactory arrangements are made by all the crown companies with the taxing authority to which each is subject.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Has any question been raised at any time by the Auditor General or otherwise as to legislative sanction for these payments, especially with respect to such payments by any of these crown corporations? While all parties have supported the policy of having grants equivalent to taxes made in respect of crown property, has any question been raised by the Auditor General, the Department of Justice or otherwise as to the need for legislation to give full legislative sanction to the making of such grants by crown corporations?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance-I am not sure whether he introduced legislation-announced in the house a policy covering the taxation of government-owned property. In that announcement he made a statement that industrial plants owned by the government would make their own arrangements, and that policy has been followed. So far as legislation is concerned, if we pass this estimate we have the legislation necessary to cover the grants this year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: That is for crown-owned property?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
My question deals with
corporations. I recall the statement of the minister to the effect that was the policy

Supply-Crown Companies that would be followed thereafter, but so far as the legal position is concerned it was done as a matter of grace and not right on the part of the municipalities. X am wondering whether any question has been raised by the Auditor General or otherwise as to payments made by crown corporations to municipalities in the absence of some clear legislative provision? I know the policy announced by the Minister of Finance, but there was no legislation introduced following his statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: My advisers tell me that we know of no objection from the Auditor General to the payments that have been made. I think the practice is well understood by hon. members through the announcement made by the Minister of Finance. He has an appropriation for that purpose covering another type of government property, and we come each year for appropriations to cover the properties owned directly by the crown. So far as the crown corporations are concerned, the payments are made with the consent of the individual board of directors. I think there is no great difficulty.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Crown companies-
82.	To provide for expenses incurred by Defence Construction (1951) Limited in procuring the construction of defence projects on behalf of the Department of National Defence, $4,242,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I should like to ask a question or two about the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. My question relates to something which took place in Halifax, so it will be obvious to members that I have been asked to raise this question by the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings, who is unable to be here at the present time. My question concerns information which came to that hon. member's attention regarding the sale of a number of Browning .5-inch machine guns which, according to the information he received, were sold as scrap. I do not know all the details, and I think perhaps the best way is to ask the minister or his parliamentary assistant whether Crown Assets Disposal Corporation sold such Browning machine guns?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: May I draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that we are discussing item 82, which deals with defence construction.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: This is quite in order, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
For the chairman's information, may I say that last evening when I sought to raise this matter on the general item it was suggested that I wait until we came to

section "B" dealing with crown companies. Did Crown Assets Disposal Corporation sell any Browning .5-inch machine guns at Halifax? If so, could the minister tell us how many and under what circumstances and on what terms?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Well, I am told that there were certain guns there sold as scrap. They were, of course, breeched and destroyed for useful purposes before they were sold as scrap. Other guns were sent to Canadian Arsenals to be rehabilitated and sold to the government of Israel.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Had those guns been sold as scrap originally? Perhaps I should ask who was the initial purchaser? My information is that it was a firm that had the word "Sumac" in the name, anyway. Were those guns sold initially as scrap and at scrap prices?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: The Sumac Company is the purchasing agency for the Israeli government. Any guns that were bought by Sumac were reconditioned by Canadian Arsenals and sold by Canadian Arsenals at what was believed to be a fair price for the account of the Israeli government. I understand that my hon. friend has asked for information on this matter, and I am told also that the Israeli government refused to consent to the information being made public. Therefore, I cannot speak about the guns that were sold to Sumac on account of the Israeli government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I understand that in conversations between the member for Annapolis-Kings and the member for Halifax, who is the parliamentary assistant to the minister, it was indicated that the Israeli government objected to the correspondence being made public. I am not talking about the correspondence. I am asking what the purchase price of those guns was which were sold to Sumac. Surely the Israeli government cannot raise objections to revealing what price the Canadian government received for those guns.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: We can get the price. I do not know that that would be a breach of confidence. We would be glad to do so, but we have not got it here at the moment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Does the minister have at the moment information as to whether or not they were sold at scrap prices or at prices which would represent a fair price for workable guns?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
They were certainly sold to Israel at fair prices which would represent the price of a workable gun. Certain guns were sold for scrap. They had deteriorated to the point where they were no longer useful, but no

guns are sold for scrap which can later be converted to useful guns. When sold for scrap, the breech is broken and they are rendered unusable. I believe we also make a kink in the barrel.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Do I understand that the price received from the Sumac Company, the price received by Crown Assets Disposal Corporation for these Browning guns under discussion, were prices for workable guns and not prices representing scrap guns?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Yes, that is correct.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I want to ask the minister one question in connection with item 82. Did his department, under this item, build the United States base at Saskatoon Mountain in the Peace river country?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I have never heard of that base. If it is a United States base, the chances are that we did not build it. If we did build it, we built it for our United States government account and I do not know that I can give any information on it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I was told that some Canadian service built it and then turned it over to the United States government for operation. I know the base has just been opened. I just wanted to know whether Defence Construction Limited had built it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Just to dispose of the matter which I had mentioned, I understand the minister is going to furnish the information if it can be done before the items carry, or if not, will give me the information later. That is as to the number of guns and the prices received.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I will furnish it later. That is a classified structure. We cannot talk about it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
National research council-
288. Salaries and other expenses, $13,536,529.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Is the minister going to make any statement on this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: No. I had not intended to do so. This is the usual estimate for the national research council. I made a statement last year about the work of the council, and I do not propose to make one at this time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
I must admit that I am greatly interested in the work of the national research council and I always find it a little bit difficult to raise any question of expense. I think that the work of this council is of great
I, 1953	4979
Supply-National Research Council importance to Canada. Our country is so far-flung and we have so many different sorts of problems arising that a research council is probably of more benefit here than it would be in any other nation in the world.
I believe that our research council has done a fine job. I notice that in the last monthly bulletin, the last NRC Research News, which is for May, 1953, one of the reports is on research into the problem of radar detection of sea ice. This research had been carried on in Hudson bay in connection with the British ministry of transport. Of course hon. members will realize just how important that research is with respect to navigation. The other report is on doughnut frying tests. That matter may be equally important and perhaps of more interest to some Canadians.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: That is to make the hole more edible.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I am not sure. I rather suspected that is what it was for.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: And we are a committee of the whole.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
In any event, I think that the research council is of great importance to the nation and that we are able to benefit greatly from its work also because we are privileged to work closely with the British and with the Americans.
Then of course it is doing splendid work in providing training for young men who subsequently go into industry. Perhaps the minister can tell us whether the policy is still one of using the research council, to a degree at least, as a training ground for experts in the various Canadian industries.
It is difficult to check the expenditures. I notice that this year the first item, which is that of salaries and other expenses, has increased by $1,337,845. I wish the minister would explain how that increase comes about.
There is one other question I should like to ask about that item and it is this. In the details at page 354, near the top of the page we find an item showing that the gross total for the continuing establishment is $8,590,284. Then there is the note "Less-Anticipated savings due to difficulty in recruiting staff". I think that was for the year 1952-53 and not for 1953-54. Perhaps the minister can explain the story behind that entry. Then the total expenditure for last year, after deducting the revenue received, was only $11,618,000, although the vote last year was for $12,198,684, the difference being made up of $550,000 received by way of revenue. How is that revenue derived? Is the item for the current
4980	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Research Council year inclusive of a certain amount calculated for revenue?
In the 1950 session we had a special committee on the research council. One year previously there had been one on atomic energy and this year the same committee, with one exception, is working on atomic energy again. I believe it would be a good practice to appoint a committee of the house to consider either one or the other each session. That would mean that perhaps next year there could be a committee-the same committee or a similar one-appointed to look into the operations of the research council.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I do not know the rules and I should like to have a statement made. May I ask if my hon. friend will tell me whether the opposition can stand with the hon. member alone?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
-to keep in touch with the workings of the national research council and Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. In that way it is possible to have some check on the moneys expended; and after all, that is an extremely important function in any democratic system of government. It is quite impossible for the members of the house to check the expenditures efficiently in the house; for example, in committee of the whole as we are today.
Then another great advantage of a committee of this kind is that hon. members are able to understand the problems being faced by the scientists engaged in this very important work. I suppose hon. members are sometimes also able to make suggestions which are helpful to the scientists. In any event it does build up a very fine feeling between the men engaged in the scientific work and the members of parliament who are on the committee in question. That has been the experience in each of these three instances, the committee on atomic energy,
I think it was in 1949; the committee on the research council in 1950; and the committee on atomic energy again this year.
It has been most interesting work for those of us who have been on the committee, and I think the result has been to give the scientists the feeling that they have the


sympathetic understanding of hon. members. In that way the welfare of the nation as a whole is promoted. Perhaps the minister can let me have a reply to some of these comments.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
My hon. friend has suggested that men go from the research staff to industry. That is true. During the past fiscal year nine have gone to Canadian industry, two have gone to Canadian universities, and four to other departments of government. These of course are senior men. The national research council does make an excellent recruiting ground for men who have been trained in scientific work, and I think in that way it performs a very valuable service.
My hon. friend asks about the increase in the appropriation. It is due to two causes; one is the somewhat larger staff and the other somewhat higher salaries. There has been a revision of salaries for technical and scientific workers during the past year, with a reaction on the appropriation. One important factor is that it is becoming the practice of government to use the national research council for special problems to an increasing extent. For instance, at the moment the council is engaged in a very extensive research into the causes of dust explosions in grain elevators. That is a big task. The council has been asked to undertake the problem of removing Ripple rock, and also-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: That is a tall order, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Yes, it takes a good deal of work. It is also studying the effect of tides on Vancouver harbour if the first narrows are dredged to a wider depth and straightened out. Special problems of that kind are being referred now to the research council and we find it is a splendid source of information.
It is difficult to get as many trained men as the establishment calls for, but if men are available, bright young men from the universities with the proper background, it is the policy to add them to the staff and thus make it possible for a turnover of staff which is helpful for scientific purposes and also very helpful to the community.
As far as a continuing committee is concerned, if I were sure that my hon. friend and I would both be back for the next session we might sort of make a definite promise, but I can assure him that if I am then the minister in charge of the national research council I will never object to a committee being appointed to examine its work. I think it is a good thing for the House of Commons and perhaps a good thing for the national research council to have a committee meet from time to time, not every year perhaps,

but at frequent intervals to examine and report on the work of the council.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
I should like to go on record as endorsing the statements that have been made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. I have been a member of this committee since it was set up some years ago. Our visits to Chalk River and Deep River have been most interesting. I support the statement made by the hon. member in connection with our visits there and the way we were received by Dr. Mackenzie and his staff. I believe that they welcomed us most sincerely, as they felt it was helpful to them for hon. members to have some information as to the work they were doing and as to some of the problems they had to encounter.
I will not go into this in detail, but the damage to the reactor last December was a most shocking thing at that time. I believe at the present time it is pretty well understood that it might have been helpful in many ways owing to the information they have been able to obtain in repairing it.
On our visit there a few years ago Dr. Lewis spoke to us at the hotel, and his information was called a gleam in the eye of the scientists. Two or three years ago he indicated to the committee the program that they had in mind at Chalk River; that is, the short-term program, and again the program with the longer vision. It was most interesting. When we went back this year he repeated some of the predictions he had made a few years ago, and went on to explain to us what had been accomplished since our last visit to Chalk River.
I feel that we have in that organization young men of vision, young men who are capable of doing a very fine job for this country. They furnish information that is greatly needed in industry in which they are playing a most prominent part. I believe that each and every member of the committee would be prepared to support their effort in every way. I must say that it is the one committee on which I have sat where there has been no criticism whatever. Every member has been prepared to do everything in his power to assist this organization, which we all consider is an asset to this country of ours. I do believe that at some future date we might expect something even more outstanding than we had up to the present time.
In so far as expenditure there is concerned, I believe that the Canadian people are convinced it is worth while, and the contribution that this country is making takes second place to none in the world.

So far the studies have been office studies. These will be available later to determine the various methods of attack upon the problem.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Borings are to be made at Ripple rock?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Not on the rock; one method would be that of tunnelling. The tunnel would have to be at a depth of, I believe, 350 feet below the surface of the water. That type of tunnelling is feasible if there is no Assuring in the rock; but if the rock were badly fissured it would be impossible to hold back the water. The drilling to be undertaken is to determine the nature of the rock.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: How can that be done? Is that not very difficult, in view of the strong currents and tides?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: The tunnelling would have to be from the shore, and under the rock. The drilling would be near the shore to determine the nature of the rock, and whether it is subject to Assuring. If it is, then that method' of attack is unworkable. If it seems to be solid rock, then the assumption would be that it would be solid rock out to and including Ripple rock itself.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: If the rock is found to be solid, when will'the actual tunnelling be begun?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Really, we are simply exploring the problem. After we find the nature of the rock we can determine as to the tunnelling. Meantime other approaches are being studied, and it is hoped a report will be made in due course, as soon as the research council can complete the data and report to the government recommending a certain manner of attack. At that time an appropriation will be made, and field work undertaken.

speechtext: Here again we have a work which is of the utmost importance to Canada, and in which we are working closely with the United Kingdom and the United States. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION

Perhaps the minister could tell us what the plans are for the reactors at Chalk River. As I understand it, the original pile which was known as Zeep is still in operation. The second pile, NRX, is the one to which the unfortunate accident happened
Supply-Atomic Energy Control Board some months ago and which I believe is now in the course of being repaired. Then we have had word of a third pile to be known as NRU. In this statement the minister is quoted as mentioning a fourth pile which has not yet been commenced but which would be used largely in connection with the setting up of power plants. Could the minister tell us what the plans are with regard to these reactors and also give us some idea as to the cost of the fourth pile?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
We are getting a good many piles here. The Zeep pile was the original one. It was a low voltage pile that was put in for experimental purposes. The commercial pile known as NRX which had been operating at Chalk River had lived its life and finally became punctured. It was believed that when punctured the life of a pile would be ended. However, it has been found possible to remove the calandria and rebuild the pile for further life. This is the first occasion this particular operation has been undertaken and it has attracted a great deal of attention both in the United States and in the United Kingdom. Scientists from both those countries have been studying the effect of operating a pile for five years and then decontaminating it and withdrawing the working parts.
That operation has now been virtually completed and all that remains to be done is to put back new working parts and start up the pile. That work is under way. The. second pile of course is the big project.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: That will be the third.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
That will be the third. When that is finished the present plans for construction of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited will have been completed as far as work at Chalk River is concerned. Methods of producing commercial power are now fairly well developed. We hope that private industry will undertake the building of a pile for the production of commercial power. That is our hope. I am not going to ask the government to build that pile because I do not think it is a proper government operation. We hope that the Ontario hydro and some of the other commercial power companies which have shown an interest in the project will combine their talents and resources to build a commercial pile. I think that that will be undertaken, but I cannot be sure just when. As my hon. friend is aware, there is a great deal of interest by private enterprise in the United States in the development of power by this method. The position is about the same in the two countries. I am hopeful that the next development will be a private industry development.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
An article in the current U.S. News and World Report is entitled "Industry Gets Set for the Atom. Sites being Chosen-Power in 2 to 5 years". The article continues:
Peaceful use of the atom is closer than you think. Private industry is ready to move in as soon as congress gives the word.
Apparently there w-ill have to be a change in the atomic energy legislation of the United States before private industry can participate. The article continues:
Electric power, generated by atomic heat, may be only two years away. That is a radical revision of the timetable.
Blueprints are being drawn for reactor plants. A hunt for sites is under way. There is a lot going on.
One startling paragraph of the article reads:
Before 1960, possibly in five years, there may be six to a dozen big-city type central power stations fueled with atomic heat at various localities in the United States.
Is the policy of the Canadian government similar to the policy which has been recommended to the United States government by their atomic energy commission, that is, that private industry be encouraged to carry most of the responsibility for the development of power from atomic energy subject, of course, to strict government control? I notice in the press of April 29 that Prime Minister Churchill states that Great Britain is setting up a new type of control. He seems to be moving in the same direction as the United States. Is the Canadian policy of the same type?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
The Canadian policy is the same as that announced in the United States, to encourage private industry to take up the development of the atom for power purposes. One difficulty in the United States is that the McMahon Act prevents any plutonium being diverted from the atomic energy commission into private hands. That restriction does not obtain in Canada. From the interest that is being taken in this matter I think we can hope that private industry in both the United States and Canada will take up the development of the atom for commercial purposes. According to the announcement by Mr. Churchill, the United Kingdom government is undertaking to build a plant which in addition to making plutonium for government purposes will also generate heat for commercial purposes. I understand that that is to be a


government undertaking, but we have no similar plans for Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: This policy will mean that private industry will develop power from atomic energy. Could there not be some policy adopted under which this power could be made available in those parts of Canada which are short of power? For example, will it be possible to have atomic energy produce power in the maritime provinces or in Saskatchewan? There should be some way by which atomic energy can be made available to those parts of Canada which do not have hydro power and which require electrical power for development purposes. Has the minister in mind any plan of that type that would help to spread industry to those parts of Canada where there is no industry at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, if this is to be a private enterprise development piles can be built anywhere. The fuel problem is not difficult; you can almost carry the fuel supply for a year or two in your hat. The shipment of fuel is not a problem. I can see that it would be more attractive to private enterprise to build in power-hungry provinces where rates would be higher; but I hope the government does not intend to get into the business of generating power from atomic energy any more than it has been in the business of developing electric power or any other form of energy.

Mr. Chairman, all this atomic energy program depends primarily on one

metal, uranium. At the present time the only uranium we are getting in Canada comes from the government mine on Great Bear lake and I believe now from Beaverlodge in northern Saskatchewan; the mine there was to come into production last month. In spite of all the rises in stocks of uranium mining companies, I understand that as yet not one ton of ore has been purchased by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited from a private company. As hon. members know, all ore must go to that company and it does seem to me that something should be done and done quickly to step up the finding of uranium and also the processing of uranium in Canada.
I think I am correct in saying that there are only two or three geologists in the geological survey branch who are available for work on radioactive minerals, whereas in the United States there are dozens or perhaps hundreds. Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, the members of the atomic energy committee were shown the laboratories where the radioactive division of the geological survey is doing its work. They are in the basement of the museum and some of the equipment cannot be used because the rooms cannot be air-conditioned; in that old building the basement apparently runs some distance on one level and then drops to another level. It is a very unsuitable place for this work.
I do believe that it is a great tragedy that this important work is being handicapped through lack of accommodation here in Ottawa. We are building a $2 million building in Washington for the joint staff, yet here in this work on radioactive minerals we make our scientists go down in a rat-hole to carry it on. I am not blaming the minister for that and I think that if he had the handling of that situation it would have been remedied some time ago-and I am not blaming the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys either.
