maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I suppose we could skip it but this is one department, Mr. Chairman, in which I am most keenly interested, chiefly because I had something to do with making some plans for health services.
On Friday last the Minister of National Health and Welfare presented to the house what he called a threefold advance. The substance of his speech was new policy as far as the federal government is concerned;
IMr. MacLean (Queens).]

and because it was new policy I felt that I should like to comment on it briefly under item 1 of his departmental estimates.
The minister spoke with considerable fervour and enthusiasm on that occasion. That, of course, is quite understandable because, when one knows that he is doing something really worth while for humanity, especially something designed to prevent or to alleviate human suffering if he has a heart at all he can wax enthusiastic when he is talking about it. That is particularly true in the early stages soon after one catches a vision of what a job there is to do and what can be done if we set our hearts to it with some determination.
I compliment the minister. He is catching a real vision, I believe, of what can be done and of what ought to be done. He has given tangible evidences of having caught it, at any rate. I think he gave no less than three of those tangible evidences when he spoke a week ago; I believe it was a week ago this very night. The minister should be encouraged because what he is now doing is, I think, right and good. People are not always given encouragement when they try to follow a vision-that is, when they set out to do what is right and good.
I know something about this matter because 16 years ago I had an intimate part in a program of a kind quite similar to the one which is now firing the enthusiasm of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, as, I may say incidentally, it is firing the enthusiasm of all of us. I recall with what fervour my colleagues and I at that time talked about plans for the provincial government especially to take over from the municipalities of our province the whole of the cost of tuberculosis treatment and of preparing the provincial department of health for an all-out fight to the finish against that dread disease. Although our total provincial revenues at that time were only $18 million, we felt that we must appropriate enough of them to provide for complete diagnosis and treatment, including medical and sanatorium care, for all the residents of our province, without direct charge to them in this fight against tuberculosis. As we saw our battle against tuberculosis succeeding, it gave us heart and determination to go further. I think perhaps the most effective single thing we did in that particular fight was to send out all over the province, into every settlement and centre, mobile X-ray diagnostic clinics. In the year 1951 these clinics alone examined 700,000 individuals, more than three-fifths of the province's total population, and that is something of an achievement.
Encouraged by the success of our fight against tuberculosis, we decided next to work

out a long-range policy covering the whole field of health and welfare. I suppose you could call it planning; it does not matter to me what you call it. In any event, it was our desire, and our hope that, in the course of making our plans and putting them into effect, we could keep them as free as possible from politics because we wanted it to develop scientifically and on a sound basis without any hasty, showy or ill-advised leaps that so often attend policies that are devised to catch votes.
I want to say right here that, as a consequence of that firm decision made early in the course of our plans, we kept the program particularly free from political influence. We decided that no part of it would be announced or put into operation just before an election, and, we stuck with that decision, Mr. Chairman. It paid off handsomely because we never had to retrace a single step and we never took a misstep in all of the progress we made in the program after the first ones were taken. There were, of course, minor changes that we made as we gathered experience, but there were no major ones. If I could be so bold as to offer a word of advice to the Minister of National Health and Welfare at this time, it would be this. The people of Canada will have much more confidence in him, in his department and in the soundness of his health program if they see his policies unfolding and developing as conditions become ready and as the provincial governments and the people are ready for advances without his relating what he does too closely to elections and vote catching.
To come back to my story for just a moment, it became our determination in the province to expand our health services program just as fast as finances could be found without imposing heavy burdens of taxation upon the people. We felt that the resources with which the good Lord had endowed our province ought to be made to pay the costs, or at any rate most of them; and this idea became part of our policy. I might say here, Mr. Chairman, that it has worked out very well because we have not instituted any health measure or measures which necessitated imposing upon the people any new taxation or any increases in old taxation measures. Very early in our experience it was recognized that, if we were to build a good, well-founded health program, our prime necessity would be hospital beds. We therefore bent every effort to get as many as possible into the province. We worked in close association with the municipalities in this area. I might say here, Mr. Chairman, that to the municipal governments must go the lion's share of the credit for the splendid progress that was made in building hospitals
Supply-Health and Welfare and in running them efficiently and cheaply, and they are still doing it. I think they are doing an excellent job from one end of our province to the other.
We had made excellent progress in this regard before the federal government entered the field with hospital grants of $1,000 a bed. But I hasten to say that the federal contribution was a real help. We acknowledge that and we are grateful that the federal government saw fit to institute these hospital grants. However, we must also bear in mind that the real heroes in the struggle to provide adequate hospital accommodation in the provinces have been the municipal taxpayers. They dig up $10,000 or $11,000 per bed for every $1,000 put up by the department of health in the province or the Department of National Health and Welfare at Ottawa.
No province in Canada can be said to have enough hospital beds today. I agree with what was said the other night in this regard by the hon. member for Lanark, who spoke in this debate and emphasized the necessity of putting forward more effort to get greater hospital accommodation in all of the provinces. As he said, more emphasis should be put on the provision of chronic patient accommodation so as to release the space these chronic cases now occupy to take care of the acute cases that need the beds. I thought a lot about that since the hon. member for Lanark spoke, and it does seem to me that one of the things toward which we should be bending our efforts today is the provision of infirmaries of some sort in connection with or quite close to old folks' homes and the like, in order to release for acute cases the beds that are now being used by the chronically ill individuals. I do not know how far the federal government can give impetus to that sort of thing in the provinces, but it does seem to me that some emphasis will have to be put on that matter in order to provide proper accommodation for acute hospital cases.
I should like to say here that no comprehensive health program in Canada is possible until our hospital space and facilities are much more nearly adequate than they are now.
I should like to revert for a moment to the earlier days of pioneering in the health service for all the people. I well recall with what enthusiasm we entered upon our polio program in Alberta. On the western prairies, as many hon. members know, we frequently suffer more or less from intense epidemics or outbreaks of poliomyelitis. For many years these outbreaks, as they came, crippled and maimed the victims. Well-meaning science seemed almost powerless to do much, if any-
4S88

Supply-Health and Welfare thing, about it. All too often the parents of the victim of the disease had not the means to pay for the long and costly treatment that was necessary, and as a consequence all too often the disease was allowed to run its course without anything being done except what could be done of course by loving hands at home.
When we experienced an outbreak of polio in 1937 and 1938 in our province our government decided to provide free medical, surgical and hospital care for all those suffering from this disease, as well as the free after-training for those who suffered paralysis from the disease. I believe I am right when I say we became in 1938 the first province to provide such a health service. I know I became most enthusiastic about it, even though I had to find the money to pay for the service, and in those days I was having plenty of difficulty to gather together enough money to take care even of the absolute necessities, let alone any frills. But I could not help becoming enthusiastic about it, as I saw suffering children and even grown-ups who became victims of the disease quickly brought into the University hospital in Edmonton to receive the very best relieving treatment and remedial training known in the world. I recall that when Sister Kenny was brought to America we did send representatives and trainees down to wherever it was she was carrying on her training course in the United States to learn her methods and bring back to the University hospital the techniques she had applied for the relief of those suffering from poliomyelitis.
Our experience in the field of polio has been a most satisfying one. Rehabilitation assistance granted to those suffering physical defects has helped many hundreds of young people especially to live useful and happy lives. Eventually we extended the same kind of rehabilitation efforts into the field of cerebral palsy. The Edmonton clinic was opened in 1950 and the Calgary clinic in 1951. They are doing outstanding work. I am sure that the provinces, particularly my province, welcome the new grants for rehabilitation services which the minister announced last Friday. It is just another evidence that the minister is seeing more clearly as the days pass the things that have to be done, and I compliment him on introducing this new service.
As I think about those days, 16 years ago, when we introduced free polio treatment and rehabilitation service, I think of how we found ourselves quite bitterly assailed by many of our political opponents for giving something for nothing. That is the kind of thing that we got. Well, that was only one of the problems
	.

we had to face in those days when we tried to do something, when we had only $18 million to $20 million total revenue out of which to do all the things we had to do. Just for the record, Mr. Chairman, we did not have oil at that time to provide the funds.
In his speech of Friday last the minister announced grants to make possible better health care for mothers and children. Here again the minister became enthusiastic, and in his enthusiasm he made some claims which will bear a little more careful examination. Amongst other things he said, at page 4681 of Hansard:
There can be no question that this federal aid over the past five years has been a factor in the decline in infant deaths in Canada from 16,333 in 1947 to 14,584 in 1951, a total saving of 10,000 infant lives In this period.
It is remarkable that we have made the progress we have in combating this terrible and unnecessary loss of human lives, and I do not blame the minister one bit for being enthusiastic about what has been accomplished, nor do I blame him for one moment for being enthusiastic about his new grants for child maternal care; but the people will hardly be able to credit those new grants with retroactive effects. Since no such grants have as yet been made, I think people generally would be more likely to believe that the remarkable decline in infant mortality in our country would have resulted from the kind of thing which we started in Alberta nine years ago; that is, in 1944.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: As I said, there already have been grants. There has been assistance along this line under the existing program.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: If that is the case, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggests to me, what is new about it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I thought I had explained that clearly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
At any rate, in 1944 we started in Alberta our fight against infant mortality by providing free hospitalization for all prospective mothers who were resident in the province, granting them free maternity hospitalization up to a period of twelve days. At present 96 per cent of Alberta's maternity cases are handled in the hospitals at a cost to the province of about $1,250,000. As I say, the program has been in effect in the province for nine years. Let me say here that it has done more than any other single thing of which I am aware to bring about a decline in infant mortality. Because of the pre-natal, natal and post-natal care the mothers get in the course of the hospitalization provided by the government, Alberta mothers have been getting along very well,

and the children have been getting the kind of start they ought to have if they are to grow to strong manhood and womanhood.
As I said, in this case the hospitalization is extended free to the mothers. This was done for the purpose of making it possible for all prospective mothers to have hospitalization. Because we discovered in our surveys taken before 1944 there were so many of the mothers who just could not afford to go to hospital some action was necessary. Of course we became very enthusiastic about it, as did the minister the other day. I can understand his enthusiasm. Our experience in Alberta leads us to commend the minister for what he is now doing. I cannot say that it is a new policy, but the procedure of extending the grants as he explained last Friday is a commendable one.
I am sure we would like to see every province in Canada providing maternity hospitalization free to its resident mothers. It can be done; there is no question about it. And, furthermore, it should be done. Under a proper financial policy our country and its resources could make that available to each prospective mother; and it should.
But if this is to be made possible, then I say much more substantial grants will have to be made available-much more than the maximum of $2 million a year proposed the other evening by the minister. And let me hasten to add that I am not belittling that amount; it is an excellent start.
One of the best fields for the government in the matter of providing health service for our people is that of diagnostic services. I believe that eventually most diagnoses will be made in clinics set up and maintained by provincial departments of health and supported by federal grants. In my opinion there is a great field here for development; and future extensions of national health policy ought to emphasize provision of free diagnostic service. We are glad to see a good start in that direction this year. I am sure that many people who today cannot get medical assistance, owing to its very high cost, will find it much easier in future to get and to pay for such medical care, provided we extend greatly government help in this field of diagnostic service. In my opinion this offers the very best field in which we could expand state health assistance.
Grants for laboratory and radiological services the minister announced last Friday will go a considerable distance in encouraging more diagnostic clinics of the kind found in some of the provinces, and which make provision for attacking cancer in its early stages, providing quick treatment for it, either by
Supply-Health and Welfare way of surgery or radium X-ray, or perhaps by the cobalt bomb. We have had such clinics in Alberta since 1940, and I understand they have had them in Saskatchewan for some years, although I do not know the exact length of time. And perhaps they are to be found in some other provinces of Canada, so that a good start has been made along this line.
We are making progress in the field of public health, but the provinces are leading the way in most branches. In my view that is a good thing. There is still much to be done, and I sincerely hope the provincial and federal departments of health will live in close harmony in laying down future policy and plans. However, this will require effort and desire on the part of the federal department as well as the departments in the provinces.
The other evening the minister was criticized for failing to use the expression "health insurance" in his speech. I listened to what was said and, as I understood it, the suggestion was that no reference whatever was made by the minister to health insurance. I am not very much worried about that, because health insurance is a term which may mean one thing to one person and another thing to another person. In short, it means different things to different people.
My colleague the hon. member for Red Deer dealt with that matter in his speech. Like him, I would like to know what people mean when they speak about health insurance- and I am not issuing that as a challenge, at all. I am merely interested to know what it is they mean. And, like my hon. friend, I would be interested in having the term defined in detail by those who use it.
The people in this country who foot the bill for these things are entitled at some time to know just what is involved when one recommends a national health insurance plan. So that if the minister does feel the urge to offer the people health insurance just prior to the general election, as the hon. member for Broadview has said he will do, then I hope he will spell out the details of that plan, including some information as to how much money his colleagues in the Department of Finance and the Department of National Revenue will have to take from the people by way of taxes to pay for this gift. I think we have got to give much more attention to the health of our taxpayers. We talk about the health of our people, but certainly we are not paying much attention to the health of the taxpayers. I am referring not only to their physical and mental health but also to their economic welfare. If we, as their legislative

Supply-Health and Welfare representatives, fail to legislate proper financial economic policies so as to make it possible for these taxpayers to keep production and distribution at a high and balanced level, we can hardly expect them to continue to bear the heavy taxes required to pay the cost of a comprehensive national health insurance program.
A great responsibility rests upon the minister when he proceeds with the investigation of his dream and vision, particularly if he is going to make taxes carry the cost of a national health insurance scheme. If he does this he will have to see to it that a broad tax base is maintained within the Canadian economy. Otherwise Canadian taxpayers may wake up some morning to find themselves ground down at the heel under a tax dictatorship. It is time the minister laid bare his plan to the Canadian taxpayers; they want and need to see what his plans are. We will go along with him on any program that is reasonable and just and that offers our people the health services they should have. But at the same time we urge that the taxpayers be given some consideration and that concurrently with the development of our health program we develop some new concepts of finance in this country to make these things possible without having the people ground down under the heels of a tax dictatorship.
There will be a number of questions I shall ask later and in order to prepare the minister for some of them I will mention now one matter which is becoming quite an issue in some parts of Canada and I should like to have his views thereon. There are certain municipalities which appear to be preparing for the fluorination of their water supplies.
I have not had the opportunity to go into the pros and cons of this mass medication, which is all it can be called, and perhaps the minister can give the committee some information during the course of the consideration of his estimates.

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry that I have not a written speech. When the minister was appointed to national health and welfare from citizenship I was very pleased because I do not think we forget that he wiped out all the little nationalities there were throughout Canada. When he was minister of citizenship he wiped out the little Italys, the little Turkeys, the little Germanys, the little Polands, the little Russias, the little Irelands and so on. Even I cannot be called an Irish-Canadian, although I like it.
Many Canadians said that the minister would be doing something worth while for Canada before very long when he was appointed minister of national health and he has not disappointed us. I am not trying to flatter him because that is the truth.


We had a debate on the question of aid for disabled persons and the minister made a promise which he is now fulfilling, or at least which he has begun to fulfil. At the next session I think we will be hearing, at least some of us, that he is more than doubling the grant for the disabled. When I brought up this resolution it would have gone to a vote if the government had not told its supporters to support it. We know that the resolution would have been carried but we accepted the minister's promise and he has kept it, just as he has kept the promise he gave before the last election that we would have old age security.
In Fort William we are grateful to the minister for the help we have received. We have been able to make an addition to the sanitarium in connection with which we received a substantial sum. An addition is being made to the McKellar hospital, and again we were given a substantial sum. When the provincial health unit was moved from the cramped quarters which it occupied in the city hall to the new wing in the McKellar hospital we again received additional assistance.
There is one thing that the people of Fort William do appreciate and that is the aid given for the training of nurses' aides. About $155,000 was provided for this purpose and a good job has been done. What is the use of having a hospital-doctors do a great job but they cannot do everything-if you do not have nurses to look after your patients. I know that these nurses' aides do a great job because I was in the hospital for a short time and I saw the service they were giving.
There are other things I would like to see brought about, such as the elimination of the means test in connection with the blind. I am not going to urge that very strongly because I said that I would not urge anything until the disabled were taken care of. I refer now to the third class of disabled. I stated before that there were three classes of these unfortunate people. There are the disabled who can get around but who cannot earn a living. There are the disabled who cannot get around but who can earn a little if they can get someone to sell the wares that they produce. Then there are the disabled who cannot earn anything, and should be given national support. You, Mr. Chairman, being mayor of your town, know who takes care of the disabled. These people must be taken care of and this represents one of the national needs of Canada at the present time. I would emphasize this much stronger if I had a better command of language.

I know that if the minister makes a promise there will be something happening. I worked for two years on the committee which drew up the details of the health insurance bill which was not put into effect. I was corrected when 1 said that the provinces did not support it. I was told that that was not true, but I think there are many Who know just who was correct. The health insurance proposed in that bill was a contributory measure. One provision that I liked, and I think the hon. member for Lanark will agree with me, was that the patient had the right to choose his own practitioner. Even a Christian Scientist could have his own practitioner. I think that is only proper because they have their rights, although I am not one of them.
I commend the minister for the present plan. I have read it over very closely and it indicates that the minister now looks after all phases of human life from the time before a person is born until he closes his eyes in sleep. But I do hope he is going to look after the disabled. We will keep after him. If I am here next year I am going to sponsor another resolution and I warn him that this time it will be carried.

Supply-Health and Welfare
As to some of the other comments made by the hon. member for Fort William with respect to old age security, blindness allowances and so on, we can deal with them when we get to the specific items.
Mr. Chairman, I did feel that something should be said1 without waiting too long by way of comment on what was said by the hon. member for Peace River with particular reference to the question of health insurance. I say at the outset that the question which he asked was a perfectly fair one. It is the same question that was asked a week ago by the hon. member for Red Deer. The question was: what is health insurance? Hon. members are perfectly right in saying that there are various forms of health insurance but it seems to me that at this stage of the debate, and at this stage of discussing this question in this country, those who speak about this matter should by now know that health insurance is one part of an over-all national health program and that it is the part that relates to providing finances for health care.
If one goes back to the green book proposals of the government of Canada to the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction, back in 1945, he will find set out therein what the government at that time called a national health program. The subheadings were: health services in Canada; health insurance; grants for planning organization; health grants; and so on. In other words, an overall health program includes a number of items. It includes grants, it includes facilities, and it includes the provision of doctors and hospitals. It also includes the question of how people are going to be able to pay for those services even after they have been made available. Mr. Chairman, it was because of the minister's omission, as far as his own speech a week ago was concerned, of any reference to health insurance that I felt that it was extremely important and a matter to which reference should be made.
I have before me the annual report of the Department of National Health and Welfare for the year ended March 31, 1952. On page 13 I find what is called an outline of the national health program. I am not going to read the program but the subheading is "Purposes of program". As I go down to the various purposes listed one of them is: "(d) to lay a sound foundation for health insurance". In other words, the government knows what health insurance is. The government knows that after you have provided hospitals, and after doctors and all the facilities are available to take care of the health of the people of Canada, there must be arrangements made for the people of this country

Supply-Health and Welfare to pay for those services. Back in 1945 the government knew that, when it made its proposals to the dominion-provincial conference. It certainly knows it now because many memoranda and monographs have been prepared on the question in the research division of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
So, Mr. Chairman, it is not my purpose to expand on the subject at this stage of the debate; but I felt I should answer the question put by the hon. member for Peace River. When we are talking about health insurance we are talking specifically about how the Canadian people are going to be able to pay for the services which are made available to them. The reason we are concerned and the reason we are exercised about the question of health insurance is that we feel that although the health grants are a real contribution to a health program for Canada, they do not pay a single Canadian's hospital bill. They do not relieve the burden of medical expense from the shoulder of a single Canadian family. These grants are welcome. They are an important step forward and we welcome them; but let them not be used as a smokescreen to try to 'hide from the Canadian people the fact that this government, which has been talking about health insurance since 1919, has done nothing about that important aspect of an over-all national health program.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Millions of dollars are being spent today seeking the cause and cure for cancer. Some day cause and cure will be discovered and humanity will be spared another great scourge that has killed many of our people in the prime of life. Tuberculosis, the white plague of a few generations ago, has been attacked by the medical profession supported by contributions from millions of people who buy Easter seals. Diabetes, thanks to the skill of two Canadian doctors who discovered insulin, is no longer the dreadful killer that it was in the past.
But rampant amongst us, virtually unrecognized and generally ignored by the public, is a common murderer known in the United States as childhood's greatest enemy. No organized body in Canada is on this killer's track. Nobody in Canada is being asked to come to the rescue and save the thousands of today's children who will be robbed of the life to which they are entitled, because of this
Supply-Health and Welfare killer's activity. For some reason or other, a disease which is the greatest known threat to our children is never publicly discussed in Canada and has never been the subject of any great, nation-wide campaign.
Rheumatic fever is generally a childhood disease. It usually begins between the ages of five and fifteen and it is the cause of most of the heart trouble in children. It is not exclusive to young ones, however. During world war II, for instance, about forty thousand men in the American armed forces were attacked by rheumatic fever.
In Canada, although no official figures are readily available, it is likely that about one hundred thousand people are affected by the disease. Not all its victims know they have it. It is a disease which may affect any part of the body, the heart, joints, blood vessels, skin or brain. Only when it attacks the heart are its effects likely to be fatal or long-lasting. Two out of three patients get well or suffer such slight damage to the heart that they can work or play like any normal person.
Rheumatic fever, next to accidents, kills or disables more school-age children than any other disease. It causes more deaths than all other communicable diseases and polio combined. Between the ages of 15 and 19 it is the leading cause of death, and between 20 and 24 it is second only to tuberculosis. When I first heard these figures, I could scarcely believe them. I could not recall ever having seen anything published in Canada which would indicate the serious damage caused by rheumatic fever. Like many others, I had heard of the disease off and on for years, but I had never thought very much about it. To me. I suppose, it did not seem to be any more important than measles, or mumps, and certainly not as serious as scarlet fever.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Yet now I find that rheumatic fever is something which should concern us all, first as a disease for the conquering of which more research needs to be done, and second, and perhaps more important, as something which can be fought with at least some success. Education is necessary. Just as in the cases of cancer, tuberculosis, and diabetes, there are weapons at hand, weapons of varying efficiency, but weapons nevertheless.

Supply-Health and Welfare
Those who are informed will use them. Those who are not informed are lucky if they do not see their afflicted ones go early to the grave. It therefore becomes the responsibility of someone in Canada to see that people are properly informed. In the United States, the American Heart Association is waging a nation-wide campaign in an effort to inform the public about the dangers of rheumatic fever. In the province of Quebec the antituberculosis league is doing similar work to prevent tuberculosis. In Canada, there is no similar campaign being undertaken, nor is there any organized group at present endeavouring to carry out similar educational work on behalf of rheumatic fever.
I bring this subject to you today, because I am convinced by the information which has now been made available to me that sometime soon something must be done to organize a campaign against rheumatic fever in this country. It will cost money and it must be thoroughly done. Perhaps this kind of program could be undertaken by some service club operating throughout Canada. No more worthy task than this could be undertaken by any club. Failing the development of interest on the part of some private branch of society, it is inevitable that the essential program will become in this country the work of a government department. The matter is too serious to leave alone. If the government, owing to public disinterest, is forced to step in, then we will have no right to complain about the danger of socialized medicine or the menace of state interference.
Apart from all humanitarian aspects, and certainly I am sure that no one in this room would reject any appeal to reduce human suffering, but apart from that aspect entirely, a program directed towards reducing rheumatic fever is well worth while. The loss of thousands of lives each year due to rheumatic fever is a serious loss to Canada, in manpower and in economic value. The training and education of a child constitutes a considerable investment by the state, as well as by his parents. The child who dies before he can return any of that investment, by contributing to the national income, must be written off as a capital loss.
Further, we never can know just what we have lost. How many of the victims might have written great books, composed great music, or painted great pictures, had they lived? How many might have contributed to Canada as scientists, as professional engineers, as business executives and builders of Canada? Those are losses we can never measure, but they are losses worth taking any precaution, spending any amounts of money, to prevent.

Fortunately, because we are friendly neighbours of the United States and because our medical leaders, our hospitals and schools work so closely together, we are able to benefit from those activities below the border. We share the fruits of their research, and we are always, in every walk of life, impressed by the generosity with which they make available to us their skills and their developments. It is consequently possible for us to do many of those things which left to our own resources would be beyond reach. An excellent illustration is provided in the campaign against rheumatic fever. I am privileged today in being able to quote to you figures and statements compiled by the American Heart Association, and to give you a basis for consideration of the situation in Canada. I am also able to give you in very brief form some of the facts about this disease, which will put you in a preferred position as compared to most Canadians, and to tell you some of the hopeful things that are being accomplished.
First of all, let me distinguish between rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease. Rheumatic fever, as I have explained, may affect any part of the body. Damage caused to the heart may be long-lasting or fatal. The effects on other parts of the body are usually temporary and not serious. Rheumatic heart disease is the inflammation and scarring of the heart muscle and heart valves as a result of rheumatic fever. This inflammation and scarring may interfere with the work of the pump that supplies the blood to our bodies, and this interference may cause death.
What causes rheumatic fever? The medical profession does not know the immediate causes. It does know, however, that rheumatic fever usually follows nose and throat infections that are caused by a germ. Those who have rheumatic fever usually have first a "strep" throat, tonsilitis or scarlet fever. Rheumatic fever usually starts two to four weeks after the "strep" disappears. Not all "strep" infections, however, are followed by rheumatic fever.
One of the difficulties faced by the medical profession in warring against rheumatic fever is that the disease has no positive symptoms all its own. Because any part of the body may be affected, the warning signals which indicate to a doctor, or to a patient, what is happening are varied. A victim of the disease may simply have a continuing pain. He may have a poor appetite, or be constantly tired. He may fail to put on weight, be pale and have repeated nosebleeds. But none of these symptoms indicates rheumatic fever alone. They may be a warning of any one of a number of other ailments.

Once a child or an adult has rheumatic fever, the lasting effects may or may not be serious. To a considerable extent, however, this is the result of luck, because there is no specific cure. Drugs, may be used to help the patient feel more comfortable, but the use of many new drugs is still experimental.
All these facts may sound very discouraging. They may lead you to question the value of a campaign against rheumatic fever because there seems to be very little we can do about it. There is, however, one bright feature about this disease. Doctors are discovering that rheumatic fever can be prevented. People who are suffering from a "strep" infection can be saved from the more serious consequences of rheumatic fever, if that first of the wonder drugs, penicillin, is given promptly. People may also be protected by improved housing conditions, by being given rest facilities and by being given early treatment. Ever since the middle of the second world war, penicillin has been produced in great quantities. It is impossible to estimate how many lives have been saved, and how many infections have been halted, because of prompt use of this wonder drug, discovered almost by accident by an English doctor.
If rheumatic fever has occurred once, the victim may be subject to relapses, each of which will endanger his life or at least make his lesions more severe. Such relapses which are always due to streptococcus may be avoided, by a continuous penicillin treatment over a period of not less than five years. Thus the patient who has had one attack of rheumatic fever is an invalid who has to be watched constantly. However, most initial attacks of rheumatic fever may be avoided in the first place by adequate use of penicillin at the first sign of "strep" infection. If such treatment is not used, it is estimated that 3 per cent of cases of "strep" infection will result in an initial attack of rheumatic fever.
That is as positive as anyone in the medical profession wants to be. We can respect them for their caution and for their wish to be sure before they make any more positive statements. But with that much indicated, with that much being considered as valid by medical people, everyone should be given the necessary information so that they can take the only apparent precaution to protect themselves and their families against rheumatic fever.
For those who have not taken such precautions and who have suffered from rheumatic fever but have recovered, there is also important information available. A child who has recovered from rheumatic fever without
Supply-Health and Welfare any apparent after-effects should be protected from future "strep" infections and should be given regular medical check-ups. In his case, sulfa drugs or penicillin, given under doctor's directions, may succeed in preventing a recurrence of the disease.
Doctors believe that much can be accomplished to reduce the death rate from rheumatic fever. They believe that teachers in the schools should be informed about it, so that they can make sure their pupils have proper medical check-ups and that parents are advised what to do. They believe that every parent should be warned about the seriousness of this disease and kept constantly on guard. They believe that by parent-doctor co-operation prevention can do away with the need for cure.
Deaths from many other causes have been reduced with a much less hopeful fund of information from which to work. Here in Canada we are making many important contributions to medical knowledge and to medical history. At the University of Montreal, and later at Ottawa University, Dr. Selye has won world-wide recognition for his research and his work in connection with nervous tension. The same can be said for Sir William Osier, on behalf of McGill University. At the Neurological Institute in Montreal patients from all parts of the world are being treated by what is probably the greatest group of brain specialists in any one centre anywhere. At the Banting Institute in Toronto, medical research is attracting world-wide attention, and at the University of Saskatchewan, preliminary work in connection with the cobalt bomb for cancer treatment drew the interest of scientists everywhere.
In one vital field we lack what is already available to people in other countries. Our medical people are doing their best, but in their fight against rheumatic fever they need more than anything else an informed public, willing and able to co-operate with them in attacking this disease before it begins; and they need organized community health programs supported by the public.
Diagnosis of rheumatic fever is so difficult and treatment is so complex, many medical men who have made a special study of this disease believe that the only possibility of success lies in a public health program, similar to the one that has been waged so successfully against tuberculosis. First of all, qualified medical consultants and clinics are required where private practitioners could seek diagnostic help and to which community agencies could send families for medical assistance. Also of great assistance would be the various types of nursing service for patients who have

Supply-Health and Welfare to be cared for at home. Social case workers to help rheumatic fever families work out such problems as better housing, housekeeping help, welfare aid, diet, et cetera, are important. The anti-tuberculosis league of Montreal, as I have stated previously, has done a wonderful job in the province of Quebec. The results achieved by this league are simply amazing.
A public health program for rheumatic fever is needed because rheumatic fever is a widespread disease; because its diagnosis depends on specialists; because its victims need prolonged treatment, and because in many cases the average citizen cannot afford all these services.
In the United States community-wide programs are being developed in many communities through the activities of the American Heart Association, the Children's Bureau, local heart associations or other agencies. By the plan adopted in London, England, under which one bed is supplied for every 550 school children, the incidence of acquired heart disease among school children dropped from two per cent to 0-8 per cent in ten years.
Figures from these community projects are encouraging because they prove that progress may be made. They also prove, however, that considerable sums of money and a great deal of effort are necessary if any achievement is to be expected. A positive, forceful, organized drive is necessary to bring home to the people of Canada the importance of doing something now about rheumatic fever.
This program is one which appeals to the hearts and to the minds of all Canadians.

They should send back far more than they are sending to the provincial governments, and they in turn should send it to the municipal governments in order to relieve the almost impossible burden of taxation, and pay the deficit through cutting unnecessary expenditures. I am not saying that most federal expenditures are not necessary. They are. I am' not one who advocates cutting out this and cutting out that when it is not necessary. The Minister of Public Works and other ministers of the cabinet will say I do not ask for any expenditures in my constituency unless they are merited and needed, and many unnecessary expenditures could be avoided.
I do believe that if the ministers would take their pencils and sharpen them they would find many items that could be cut out, and the money thus saved could be given to the Minister of National Health and Welfare for distribution to the provinces and to the municipalities, thereby lessening the burden of heavy taxation that has to be carried for essential hospitals. In that way these hospitals could rely more on federal taxes. That is all I want to say. That can be done; it has to be done; we should have no more procrastination. Federal grants to municipal hospitals should be greater. They are all part and parcel of this great dominion of ours.

262.	Administration of the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, $157,773.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Item 262 is for administration of the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act. I should like to give the minister a few suggestions with regard to this particular problem. It is of great concern on the west coast, as the minister is doubtless aware. In his annual report, at page 130, I find a list of the convictions under the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act for the judicial year ended September 30, 1951. In that period of twelve months there were 376 convictions under the act in Canada. Of that number 205 were in British Columbia. I presume that is because of our proximity to the Orient. No doubt it is easier to get the drugs in by way of the west coast of Canada than it is by the east.
However, the situation there has hecome quite alarming. As a matter of fact within the last two or three weeks 31 suspects have been picked up for trafficking in drugs. This is the largest group of su'spects rounded up at any one time in Vancouver. I have here the figures showing the numbers of convictions down through the years. In 1941 there were 58 convictions in Vancouver. In 1948 that was up to 158. In 1951 there were 222; and for the calendar year 1952 there were 334.
I am told on reliable authority that the Vancouver police narcotics squad claim personal knowledge of 1,400 addicts in the city of Vancouver. The situation has become so serious that last year the community chest and council set up a special committee to study the drug situation. They made extensive investigations, and eventually submitted a brief to the minister.
What they are asking is clearly set out in a letter I received from Dr. Wallace Wilson, who was then president of the community chests and is a past president of the Canadian Medical Association. While this is a private letter I believe it would be helpful if I were


to read one or two paragraphs from it, because in it Dr. Wilson outlines the thinking by the committee on this problem. He says:
We do want the maximum penalties increased for the trafficker whose sole purpose is to make money, and who often or usually is not an addict himself.
What he is referring to is penalties under the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act. He says:
We do want the drug addict whose only offence is addiction treated as a medical case and not as a criminal.
That, I think, is a significant recommendation. Then he says:
We do want to see established a treatment centre where suitable screened volunteers can receive treatment. But in order that treatment may be satisfactory there must be authority whereby, once the addict volunteers, he can be detained in the treatment centre for the required period of time. We do believe that if an addict who was found to be incurable could receive his maintenance dose at a supervised government clinic at a comparatively few cents' cost it would eventually knock the bottom out of the black market traffic.
Those are very far-reaching recommendations. I believe that in Great Britain they now have a system in line with the last recommendation, that is, a government clinic at which drugs are sold to these addicts at a very low price. The recommendations of the committee were approved in practically every respect by the British Columbia medical association last year, so the full weight of medical opinion on the west coast is behind these recommendations. But nothing whatever can be done along these lines unless there are amendments to the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act; because that act makes it a crime, for example, for a doctor to carry out some of these recommendations. Steps of this kind simply cannot be taken without amendment to the act.
We have been hoping on the west coast that the minister would see fit to bring in an amendment at the present session. Obviously that is now impossible. But I had hoped that something could be done to study this whole situation, so that at the next session of parliament, no matter who may form a government, amendments could be made to the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act.
There is also the suggestion in the brief that provision should be made for research into the problem. The provincial government has offered to permit research in the provincial jails, and I believe that the University of British Columbia is prepared to carry on the actual work. But this will require a grant from the dominion government. There would seem to be no reason why that part of the recommendation could not be carried out, without legislation. As one of our magistrates in Vancouver put it to me in a letter received within the last

few days, the crop of addicts seems to be growing daily; yet the thinking here in Ottawa on this problem continues to run in the same old groove.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I hope I can show my hon. friend that that is not so.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
That is the opinion that has been formed on the west coast, and I hope it is wrong. However, I am told there is a feeling that nothing is being done here in Ottawa, and that the tendency is here to follow the same old line that has been taken for a great many years, to remain oblivious of the seriousness of the problem.
According to press dispatches the minister promised action last July, over nine months ago. But we believe a new approach is required, and that action must be taken quickly. I am afraid that the attitude of, perhaps, the whole of eastern Canada indicates that there is no clear realization of the menace contained in this situation. It is only a matter of time until other seaports in Canada will be faced with the same problem. As the country grows, and as international trade increases, more and more shipping will be entering our ports, and the problem will become more serious.
Younger and younger persons are becoming addicts; the drug is reaching younger groups all the time. It is a problem which cannot be ignored. I would hope that the minister could give the committee some assurance today that he realizes the seriousness of the situation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall hold up the committee but a moment, but I do want to say that I support in a general way the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. The people of Vancouver and I imagine of the rest of the province of British Columbia are alarmed over the growth of the drug traffic in our province. Both the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and I were invited to become members of the narcotics committee which was set up last fall, but unfortunately-for us, not for the committee-we have not been able to attend and thus have the benefit of the discussions that took place.
It was found last fall that the drug traffic had got into our high schools. I do not want to give the impression that great numbers of children attending the high schools were becoming drug addicts, but a certain number were found to be victims. I appreciate that there are two schools of thought as to the proper way to deal with these unfortunate victims of drug addiction. There is a new school which believes that in order to bring about a cure the drug addicts should be given small doses of the drug. I think that is the
Supply-Health and Welfare proposal referred to in the report endorsed by the medical association of British Columbia. However, strong exception was taken to that by a man named Wilson, who I believe is a retired R.C.M.P. officer with considerable experience. That being so, one would have to give serious thought to what he said.
I am not expressing any opinion as to the method that should be adopted, but something should be done. I appreciate that the act cannot be changed without considerable research being carried on. I was going to ask the minister if it was contemplated to change the act in the near future. I am sure the people of British Columbia will be looking forward and hoping-it may get beyond hope and reach the stage where they will be demanding-that something be done to help them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, no doubt the reason for this increase in drug addiction in Vancouver is due to the fact that so many ships come into that port after crossing the Pacific ocean. Because of our increased international trade we are exposed to things like this drug addiction. This is something which should be taken up vigorously by the United Nations. Probably they are dealing with it at the present time. I am sure that all members of the United Nations would join in a campaign against the sale and distribution of narcotics. I think even Russia would show an interest in joining with other nations in trying to stamp out this evil.
Of course Asia is the centre of production of opium, and has been since time immemorial. We have heard of the goings on in Indo-China and the need of certain military action, but I do not think it is generally known that the sale and distribution of opium is openly tolerated in Indo-China under the French government, or was until quite recently. It is not generally known that the sale and distribution of opium is legalized in Malaya. The stuff is sold in vendors' stores just as liquor is sold in Ontario. I think the same is true of Hong Kong, or was until recently. There were stores there where these drugs could be obtained.
If those conditions exist on the other side of the Pacific ocean it is quite obvious that the ports of British Columbia will be exposed to trafficking in opium and its derivatives. That is just what is happening in Vancouver. Our trade with Asia is increasing, and this is part of the penalty we have to pay.
One thing we can do to stamp out this traffic is to increase our efforts in the way of education. This is something that should be taken up by the churches and the schools so that our children may be warned of the dangers of narcotics. I do not think the

Supply-Health and Welfare Asiatics are entirely to blame for flooding our country with this stuff because there are people here who are glad to make money from the sale of painkillers and sleeping potions and tablets which are supposed to be harmless and which have to do with encouraging sleep.
We should be wary about allowing our children to have anything in the way of painkillers or these tablets that are sold and advertised, possibly over the radio. Education should be carried on along these lines. Somebody mentioned cigarettes this afternoon. When boys and girls of juvenile ages indulge in that habit they are making it easy for someone to come along and give them some other form of sedative which might lead ultimately to the use of narcotics.
There are two ways to approach this problem. One is through education in the schools, in the churches and in the homes. This iniquitous habit of parents leaving their children of tender years at home nights in the care of baby sitters while they go gadding about may very well be a source of difficulty in regard to this. There is always the temptation to give a child something to make it sleep so it will not be an annoyance. I say that education should be started in the homes and carried on through the schools and churches. A great stroke of work could be done by the United Nations, and I think men like the minister who are familiar with this narcotics problem should marshal the representatives of the other nations so this evil may be stamped out.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this matter is so important that I feel I should say something. I agree with the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, that the basic cure for this problem, as for all problems involving human beings, is the character of our people. Character is moulded by the right kind of influences. The United Nations, following what was done by the league of nations, is attempting to deal with the world opium and narcotic drugs traffic. We have had Colonel Sharman as our representative on that body for many years, the former chief of our narcotic division. He is recognized as one of the most eminent men among the many countries who are signatories to the convention. His work is now being supplemented by the head of the division, Mr. Hossick. I may tell my hon. friend that at the first meeting of the economic and social council of the United Nations, one of the first things done was to plead with certain countries, notably the Soviet union, not to allow political ideology to stand in the way of their adherence to the convention on the


international restraint of the opium and drug traffic.
To come to the specific matter, all hon. members from British Columbia have at one time or another mentioned the problem now introduced by the hon. member for Vancou-ver-Quadra. Last summer when this question was brought to a head and when extraordinary interest was displayed in Vancouver, we had an immediate conference with the government of British Columbia. I think the way we will solve this problem, if it is going to be solved, is by way of recognizing its difficulty, as the hon. member for Vancouver East did today. It is an extremely difficult problem, one that civilization has been dealing with for a considerable time. No amount of impatience will bring about a solution. What has to be done is explore every avenue, and that is what is being done.
The problem is criminal in its aspects, and health is involved in its direction. The direct aspects of health, of course, come under the provincial governments. The problem has been approached in this way. Immediately after the action taken pursuant to the community investigation the head of the legal division of our narcotic division and the head of our mental health division journeyed to Vancouver and conferred with the committee, with the provincial government, with police bodies and with others in an attempt to bring the question into focus for discussion and consideration, and if possible for decision.
As was announced in this house over a year and a half ago, in the narcotic and opium division we have been paying special attention to some work that is being done, notably in two institutions in the United States. I can now give some conclusions about our visits and discussions in connection with those two institutions. The problem is not going to be solved, in our mind-there is disagreement on this point, but we might as well be frank-by putting more drugs at the disposal of addicts. We would think that would be as unwise an approach as it would be to put more alcohol at the disposal of alcoholics.
The best practical opinion we can get in all these countries where the problem has been considered supports the view that I have just indicated. Experiments have been attempted in this country and in other countries with that very matter, with inconclusive results. In one of the European natrons the problem has been very carefully examined from that point of view, but the abuses were so great as to require that a change of policy be made at once.

The other suggestion is that drug addicts -and I am now talking of the non-criminal drug addicts-should be placed in institutions where, under medical and other supervision, the greatest degree of attention can be paid to them. There are two such institutions in the United States, one at Fort Worth, Texas, and one at Lexington; and a smaller institution in New York city which attends to young addicts. I have visited both institutions, the one at Fort Worth and the one at Lexington, and so have my -officers. Within the last six weeks I have conferred with two gentlemen who have had great experience in this particular work at one of those institutions. Since one has to exercise responsibility, we have come to the conclusion that the cost of maintaining an institution in this country similar to the two I have mentioned would not be justified by the experience of those institutions.
They were set up for the laudable and ideal purpose of trying to cope with this problem, but I am safe in saying that they have not measured up to expectations. One should not close one's mind completely, and I am not closing my mind completely. I am saying that the best possible technical assessment that can be made of the problem does not justify the conclusion that this is the way to deal with the problem. We are continuing our observations of the two institutions, and considering other suggestions that are being made.
The other suggestion is that the criminal addict should be controlled, segregated, and brought under the direct attention of doctors and others who have had experience with this problem. I can only say that we have yet to make a final assessment of that phase of the whole problem, and I would not want to make a final prediction on it. I do know that in other countries where it has been attempted the success of the measure has not been what one, a priori, would think would have been the case.
Well, that is the problem. It is not as serious as it is sometimes made out to be, but it is an important problem and we all recognize it- as such. It is one of the most unfortunate things in the world to see healthy human beings resort to drugs for one purpose or another. One does feel, particularly in the position that I hold, not helplessness- that would not be the word; perhaps "baffled" would be better-and I have given it the greatest personal attention, but one would be very happy if one could in some small way contribute to the solution of this problem.
We do have some views on the matter and on what for the present we have decided to
Supply-Health and Welfare do. We have already advised the government of British Columbia that,we are undertaking a survey in that province almost forthwith. I use the word "survey" although I do not know that it is the accurate word, but it will be an examination of this whole problem. We are seeking to get the history of every patient, of every drug addict, criminal or non-criminal, and to go into the byways and do other things which I would not want to speak about publicly. The government of British Columbia has been so advised. The survey will be made with their assistance and at our complete expense, recognizing that we have a responsibility in this matter. They too recognize, of course, that the health aspects are primarily theirs. I may only hope that our combined efforts in this field will enable us some months hence to say that we have made some advance. Whether we do or not, I want my hon. friend and others to know that it will not be because we have not continued to try.

There are hospitals where doctors treat certain patients, and where the principle of withdrawal is followed. Generally speaking, there is no institution in the world where that practice is successfully carried out. There are individual experiments being carried out by our research people, but generally speaking no drug addict in Canada should expect that any health department in this country will encourage his addiction by giving him or her any more drugs.

speechtext:
During the past seven years, year by year, we in this house have voted a constantly increasing amount of money for Indian health services. This general increase in the grants made has been reflected in a gradual improvement in the Indian health service, the provision of hospitals for our native population and the amount of medical aid they have received. This has resulted in a considerable improvement in the general health of the Indians, a reduction in the tuberculosis rate, and so on.
During the past year, however, I have received complaints that the provision of health services to Indians has been terminated in some cases, and in other cases lessened to a certain degree. In other words, there appears to have been a tendency recently on the part of the Department of National Health and Welfare to gradually withdraw health services from our more prosperous Indian bands. I would cite what has happened in the case of two or three bands, and ask the minister to answer specifically as to why these services have been withdrawn and just what is the general policy.
As I say, the tendency appears to be a gradual withdrawal of medical services from the bands that are more prosperous than they were a few years ago. If that is the case, I think it is a backward step which will cause deterioration in the health of the Indians and get us back to the condition which existed seven or eight years ago, before this improvement took place. One of the bands in which this has happened is what is known as the Enoch band, or the Stony Plain, of Alberta, west of Edmonton. I do not know whether or not oil was actually found on their land, but at any rate they received certain payments from an oil company. Following that, orders were issued that only those services which are ordinarily free to Alberta white residents, such as maternity care, tuberculosis treatment and so on, were to be continued free to the Indians of this band, and that it would be necessary from now on for those Indians to pay for all medical attention other than that to which I have referred.
The situation is that these Indians are not in a position to pay for these services. If a white man cannot pay his medical expenses, he is able to fall back on the municipality. These Indians have no municipality to fall back upon, and when this department refuses to look after them they are without medical services. They have no other place to go.

Another point is that along the shores of Lesser Slave lake where there is no Indian hospital, there is a Roman Catholic hospital at High Prairie which looks after a certain number of these Indians; but Lesser Slave lake is quite a long lake, and many of these Indians are a long way from medical attention in the towns or villages. They are required to pay for this medical attention themselves. Once more, these Indians are poor. They are in no position to do so.
We come now to the position of the Black-foot band east of Calgary. The Blackfoot band were in a better financial position than any band in Alberta, perhaps in Canada, at one time. They had a certain amount of revenue, and they built a hospital themselves out of their own funds. They provided the money to run this hospital, although I think the Indian department paid for a doctor. Apart from that, the Indians paid for the building and running of a hospital. These Indians have encountered the same problem that other people operating hospitals have encountered. In other words, costs have increased for them just as they have increased for other people, and the running of this hospital has now become a burden greater than they can readily carry. Their revenues are not as buoyant now as they used to be, as a matter of fact. The operation of this hospital worked out at a cost to them of $30 a head per year for those Indians.
Most of those Indians have little income. The thing has therefore become too much of a burden to them. They cannot understand why they, of all the Indians in the west, should be the only ones to have to maintain their own hospital. They have made this request several times. I am sure it has been brought to the minister's attention. I know I myself have brought it to the attention of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, and no doubt it has come to the attention of the minister. These Indians on various occasions have requested that the government should treat them in the same way it treats other Indians, and should pay at least part of the costs they now have to meet in operating this hospital. In fact, they think they should be on the same basis as the others, and that the government should take over the hospital and run it the same as they run other Indian hospitals. I think the time has come when some action along that line needs to be taken.
As to the policy that appears to be followed now in Alberta, namely that of throwing the Indians on their own resources in matters of health, the only result can be a deterioration 68108-316
Supply-Health and Welfare in the health of the Indians and hence an increase in the death rate among those people. Their death rate is already much higher than that among the rest of the people of Canada. I fervently hope this development will be brought to an end, and that the department will move back to the policy it followed up to at least last year, as far as I can make out. If the minister will comment on some of those matters, particularly this matter of policy in public health, I have some questions I should like to ask him.

I should like to ask the minister whether there is co-operation with the Department of Transport as to communications away back in the hinterlands where Indians reside. At Finlay Forks there was at one time a radio station which provided communication between that point and the nearest doctor, who would be perhaps 200 or 300 miles to the south. That radio station has been discontinued. I do not know whether it was operated through co-operation with the health department. But where those communities are back in the wilderness, many miles away from a hospital and medical care, I think we could afford to maintain those telephone and radio services.
Finlay Forks is a central point there. While the health of the Indians has been greatly improved in the last few years, especially where they are easily accessible from the highways, the rivers and so on by which the doctors and health nurses go in, farther back, in places like Finlay Forks, the matter of getting in is a costly one. Transportation is usually by aircraft. The existence of a radio station there would be highly necessary to the health of those Indians.

I note the wellmeaning observations of the hon. member for Calgary West. We have made an endeavour, as our budget indicates, to try to do something about Indian health. Both my predecessor and those who have served in the department under me have, I think, a record of which we may be extremely proud. By an increased budget, which began at $800,000 and is now over $14 million, we are seeking to improve the health standards of our native population. A United Nations publication recently referred to Canada's health services for Indians as the most outstanding in the world. That is an appraisal of which we are very proud.
As to the particular case which my hon. friend mentioned, if that lone Indian could not afford it and was not in a place where she could get immediate attention, we would see that she got it. That is not our constitutional obligation, but we regard it as our moral obligation.
With regard to Indians who can pay, may I say frankly that we are embarking on a policy of asking them to pay for services rendered. I think that is only common sense. There are not many Indians in that category. But this situation was brought to my attention one


day in British Columbia. An Indian father whose income, on his own admission, was over $30,000-he was an extremely rare individual, but this is an actual case-was insisting on and was actually getting free medical assistance at our hospital for himself and his family. I did not regard that situation as being fair to the people of Canada generally or to other Indians in Canada who are not yet given the services that we want to see given them. This policy does not cover very many. If my hon. friend can bring forward any case of any Indian who is in necessitous circumstances and is unable to get the best of treatment, I should like to have his name. I may assure my hon. friend that such a case would receive our immediate attention.
I said that we were achieving something in what we were doing to try to improve the health of our Indian population. Five years ago we began a program to try to cut down the incidence of tuberculosis. That was the reason for building that hospital of ours up in the wilds of James bay; and we have followed that one with hospitals that we have built elsewhere. In 1948 the tuberculosis death rate per hundred thousand for Indians was 488-5; in 1949 it was 399-6; in 1950, 298-8; in 1951, 268-2; in 1952, 253. Gradually year by year we are cutting down the tuberculosis mortality rate among our Indian population. It is not as good as it is among the white population because we began late, but my hon. friend may be sure that we are embarking upon a policy of bringing improved health to the native population of our country.

I would like the minister to give some definite undertaking that these Indians will be put on the same basis as other Indians. They have not been put on the same basis as the other Indians in Alberta, or anywhere else in the country. There are only two places in Canada where Indians have to pay all their medical expenses. One is at the Six Nations reserve at Brantford and the other is this Blackfoot reserve east of Calgary.
The excuse which has always been given to me as to why the Blackfoot have had to pay for all their own medical attention was that they had some money to do so, and they were in the same position as the Six Nations. They were not, because they are in a position by themselves. To try to put these two groups of Indians on the same basis is just ridiculous. The Indians at Brantford have been in touch with white men for some two or three hundred years longer than the Indians east of Calgary. It is only for the last 75 or 80 years that these Indians have been in contact with white men at all, except for the odd traveller or fur trader who went through that country. As a result, they are at least 200 years behind in the development of contacts with white civilization and the adoption of white ways and so forth. They are that much behind the Six Nations Indians. It is absolutely unfair, and it is no argument at all to say, well, the Six Nations have to pay for their own hospitalization, why cannot these people?
