subtopic: LIONEL JOBIN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I can assure hon. members who are interested in the passage of this divorce bill that I am not going to use my traditional right to prevent it passing the house, but I do have a word or two to say in regard to it because there are certain circumstances which I think should be placed before the house. In the first place,
5008	HOUSE OF
Private Bill-Divorce
so far as I can judge this is one of those divorces which has been inspired by the fact that the petitioner, after a long number of years of separation, has now been compelled to pay a living allowance to his wife. Of course that has no effect upon the law of the land. I want to relate the facts of this case to emphasize the inadequacy of the divorce machinery that we have in this parliament.
This bill was contested and for that reason it held some interest for me because, as I have stated before, when a contested divorce bill comes before this parliament and no evidence in connection therewith is produced, as a matter of principle I will vote against it until I see evidence which justifies me voting for it. Perhaps these things are hurried along because we are nearly at the end of the session, but at any rate we had a notice sent to us that the committee on miscellaneous private bills would meet to consider this bill.
We did meet and there was a small attendance at the committee. I pointed out on that occasion that the evidence had not been distributed. It is true that there was one typed copy of the evidence in the hands of the clerk, but no member had received a copy nor was the evidence available to counsel who wished to plead the case. When the committee met I suggested an adjournment until we had an opportunity to study the evidence, but my wish did not prevail. Most members of the committee decided to proceed and the committee proceeded. Both counsel were invited into the committee room. The main argument of counsel who was looking after the interests of the respondent was that he had no evidence in his hands, that he had nothing to refer to and therefore had nothing to plead.
In spite of that the majority of the members of the committee decided to proceed and they did proceed. To the astonishment of some of them, when the chairman put the preamble to the committee it failed to carry. I think the vote was 7 to 5. The bill was killed by that vote. There was a bit of a stir in the committee, but I was sitting next but one to the chairman and I heard him say, "Well, that is the end of that". I assumed that that was the end of that particular divorce bill, and that the divorce was killed.
Therefore I was astonished that evening to receive another call to a meeting. I telephoned the chairman and he told me, "The purpose of this meeting is that I omitted to say to the committee when it rose this morning 'Shall I report the bill?' You are being brought back to regularize the action of the committee this morning." When we


got down to it we discovered that the situation was largely as it had been before. One member of the committee got up and moved that the committee revert to consideration of the preamble, which as hon. gentlemen know simply meant that we would reopen the whole matter. I opposed that action, but the committee decided to consider this divorce plea again. I again moved the adjournment of the committee until such time as we had the evidence and had had an opportunity to study it. This time I found my colleagues friendly to that idea. There was no doubt that the evidence would be available and they would be able to consider it next morning at ten o'clock.
We did consider the matter again next morning at ten o'clock, and I was surprised to find that many more members of the committee were taking an interest in this divorce. We had had little time to study the evidence. The evidence had come to my hand just ten minutes before dinner time, and that was why I had moved the adjournment.
We must go on to the third meeting of the committee. The evidence had been distributed. Someone had taken good care of that. Someone had even had the evidence mimeographed downstairs so no one could .say that he did not have it. By a coincidence the regular booklet of evidence came in from Toronto or from wherever it was being printed just a few minutes later, so at the final meeting of the committee we had the evidence.
I should like to point out that this error of the chairman-I do not mind using that term because he admitted it-was a particularly fortuitous omission. Of course I would never suspect the chairman of the present committee of doing anything like that deliberately but I would point out that it might be possible for a chairman who believed in the minority side in that first vote to have omitted to put that question to the committee and so force another meeting of that committee, compel it to reopen the matter and have it considered by people who were in favour of his own side of the case.
Let me make it perfectly clear that I make no such charge. My simple purpose is to show the fallacy and foolishness of this whole business of trying to handle this matter of divorce in such an inadequate way which does not do justice to anyone. You can see how the fate of individuals sometimes hangs by a thread. Here was a woman who had received news from her lawyer saying that her case was won. Then the next day she hears that the decision has been reversed. Does that look to anyone here like sensible

business, to have a decision reversed by what was largely a different group of men? It is true that there were a few who had attended the previous meeting, but on the whole it was a different group of men. It was at an entirely different meeting of the committee that the decision was reversed. This is an important case in so far as this is concerned.
And now in conclusion, for I must hurry along; I want to be democratic in the matter -as I said I know that I could have connived to hold up this divorce, but I do not think that would have been democratic procedure. At the last meeting of the committee-and it was the last one after all-it was decided that the divorce should be granted, and so be it. But I want to point out that this whole system is wrong. Incidentally, I was interested and surprised to see that some of my hon. friends from the province of Quebec, who have never before, as far as I have observed, taken part in divorce cases, were yesterday advocating the passage of this particular divorce. Let me say to them that we would by no means ever wish to force a divorce court upon any province which did not wish to have it because of religious beliefs.
However we do, as members of parliament, want to get rid of this thing, this iniquitous thing; because I believe it is that. Personally, and I know that some of my friends do not agree with me, I do not see how one's conscience would be violated any more by having a court try divorces-for instance the court across the road, the exchequer court in Ottawa-than it is by having the present procedure which makes this parliament, to all intents, a divorce court for the province of Quebec and for Newfoundland.
Another thing is that I feel, if I am to be asked to judge divorces, that I should consider the cases and give them some thought. This year we have not done so. Last year some people in this party, and it is not a party matter or a political matter, did try to examine some of these things in the house. It was simply impossible. This year we have passed three or four hundred of them- I do not know what the exact figure is- but outside of this case and one other I know of, no divorce case has been given any individual consideration.
I wrote down the length of time it took in the committee to pass 67 divorce cases, or 58 of them

I would not want to be quoted as to the number-and they were going through at the rate of half a second each. That is all right if we are not supposed to consider these cases; but it is part of our duty to decide whether or not a divorce should be granted. As far as I am concerned
Private Bill-Divorce
I do not want to have this thing on my conscience any more.
I was reminded frequently by one of my hon. friends that I am not a lawyer. Granted; but may I suggest to him that this is not supposed to be a committee of lawyers, it is supposed to be a committee of ordinary men who represent the people of the constituencies in this country. As such a representative I admit I have no legal talent, but at least I have a certain amount of common sense.
Well, that is the situation. Each session I protest against this sort of thing but up to now, and I presume now too, I have protested without avail. That is my case. This thing should be removed from the House of Commons-apart from the particular method by which this divorce was handled, the decision made, the technical error on the part of the chairman, and the reversal of that decision.
Well, there it is.

maintopic: PRIVATE BILL
subtopic: LIONEL JOBIN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am happy in one way to follow my hon. friend from Saskatoon and support him in his argument in respect of the manner in which this bill went through the committee, and in his protest in respect of the way these bills are dealt with in this house instead of in a separate court. On the other hand, I am rather unhappy to have to get up here and talk about such divorce bills as come before us. However, we are on the private bills committee, and our parliamentary procedure, such as it is, makes us duty-bound to attend and do what we can when we once submit to our names being placed on committee.
Mr. Chairman, while this bill was in the process of discussion in the committee, and when the peculiar incident took place of being recalled to reconsider our decision, I told the committee that I did not think I could permit the bill to go through in the manner in which it was being handled without having something to say in the house. The particular reason I rise on this occasion is to protest the action of those in the committee, some of them in particular, in attempting to reverse the decision that had previously been made.
My hon. friend from Saskatoon has told the story. I am just going to tell the story again in perhaps, if I may say so, a little more picturesque way. The committee was called together in the morning-pardon me, I have got it wrong. I think the bill was presented to us at the evening session, but it does not make any difference. We discussed the bill. The chairman of the committee called section 1-, section 2, and so on. Then he came to the part "Shall the preamble carry?".

Private Bill-Divorce
That, as we all know, of course, is the crux of the whole bill. If the preamble is rejected, that is tantamount to killing the bill. However, just as the chairman called "Shall the preamble carry?" the bells calling us to this chamber began to ring. We looked at one another and said, "There are the bells; we will have to go. If we do not deal with the preamble we will have to come back again and deal with it later." The cry went up from the members: "Let us have the vote now. Let us have the vote now." Let me say that cry came from some of those who demanded that the thing be reconsidered later. They said: "Oh, yes; let us have the vote now". So the chairman said: "Shall we take the vote?" and "All right; those in favour of the preamble raise your hands". Well, some raised their hands. "Those opposed put up your hands". And what happened? The preamble was defeated, to the surprise of some of those who had said: "Let us take the vote now". So of course the chairman said, "Well, that fixes it" or "That is the end of it" or a phrase of that kind. We did not even stop to listen carefully to the phrase which the chairman used. The bells were ringing and a vote was to be taken so everybody scampered out, and that was the end of that.
Well, to our surprise in the mail we got our usual little notice calling the private bills committee together with the comment on the top: "To consider the Jobin case". I said to myself: "Why, we considered that before. That is all done. That bill was killed in the committee". So we went back and the chairman asked the clerk to read the minutes of the meeting, which he did; and the chairman began to indicate that he had failed to use- and this is it-the little phrase "Shall I report the bill?"
That was all; he had failed to say that. The fact of the matter is that the bells were ringing and he said, "That is the end of that; that killed the bill." Well, someone rose and said we must consider whether the chairman is to report the bill and "I therefore move that we reopen the preamble." Here was the same committee sitting on another day with a slight change in personnel because there were more members attending the meeting that day than there were previously when the vote was taken. My hon. friend says there were twice as many.
What does that represent to you, Mr. Chairman? It is obvious that some members got together and said, "My, that bill should go through." Some members said it had been killed, so they scratched some hair out and said, "What are we going to do about this? We have to get this thing through." Someone

grasped on that very slim thread of technicality in that the chairman had not said, "Shall I report the bill?" It was then decided to call the committee together so he could say, "Shall I report the bill?"

speechtext: On a question of privilege-

maintopic: PRIVATE BILL

On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I believe the hon. member is again stating that the meeting was called for the purpose of permitting this procedure which he has fully described. I must explain, because the hon. member has repeated it twice, that the meeting was called because the clerk of the committee had reminded me that the technicalities had not been complied with. It was not only because the question "Shall I report the bill?" had not been

put. There were still further things that had to be put, which did not come up because the decision of the committee was reversed.

maintopic: PRIVATE BILL
subtopic: LIONEL JOBIN
speechtext: The chairman of the committee has explained his position, and that is all right. Whether or not he called the committee together in order to regularize the procedure, I am not debating that. That is what he did. But in reality the committee was called together to reverse the decision. The hon. member for Lake Centre asks if this procedure had been followed before. I say that, to my knowledge, that has never happened before' in the private bills committee. The hon. member for Halton rose in the committee and said that he had been chairman of many parliamentary committees, and they often reversed a previous decision on a clause or something of that kind. Perhaps that is so, particularly if they reversed the decision on the same day. But when a bill has been killed in a committee and the committee adjourned because a vote was being taken here, and then was not recalled, it is understood that the end of the bill has been reached and a decision made. maintopic: PRIVATE BILL

maintopic: PRIVATE BILL

speechtext: It did happen this time, Mr. Chairman. There is no question in the world in my mind-I do not want to cast reflections-but that someone was instrumental in getting the committee recalled with the one purpose in mind of changing the decision.

That is laying it right on the line.
Let me say this. There might be some real reason why a thing of this sort should 68108-317

be done if it were the reversal of some government policy, but this is a private bill. The government is not going to stand or fall upon some individual getting a divorce. I have said enough. I think the chairman is a fine fellow. I think he conducts the business of the committee very well. I am not even saying the chairman made a mistake. I wish to say just a few words on this bill. First of all, being a Catholic, I do not accept any dissolution of marriage vows. I would accept an annulment given by the proper authorities of my church, but nothing else. In the second place, I was not a member of this committee; but if there were members from the province of Quebec on this committee, they certainly did not vote for the annulment of the marriage vows. According to the constitution, divorce bills must be dealt with by the federal authority. Of course our civil code in Quebec does not admit dissolution or annulment of marriage. Those who were in this committee on divorce, if they participated in the voting, voted for the dissolution of the civil contract, not of the marriage in itself.
The hon. member for Saskatoon took notice of the fact that members from the province of Quebec were in this committee. What I wanted to tell him was that we do not believe in the annulment of marriage vows. If those members voted, they voted for the dissolution of the civil contract and nothing else. As to the second clause of the bill, it says that this man has the right to remarry. We cannot accept that clause of the bill.

maintopic: PRIVATE BILL

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as a member of the committee I want to voice my protest at the procedure which was followed. I

Private Bill-Divorce
think what has happened in this case is simply another example in favour of the plea which we in this group have been making over the years, namely that it is high time this whole question of divorce was removed from the jurisdiction of this parliament.
I am not going to argue for or against this case. I am satisfied in my own mind that one of the parties in the case set out deliberately to trap the other and succeeded in doing so. I am satisfied that if this case had ever come before a regular court of law, the divorce would not have been granted. However, what I want to say is that the situation was rather unusual. Let us grant that the chairman had made an admission that he had omitted calling out whether he should report the bill, and let us grant that he was right in calling the committee back the next day. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, May 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Knowles for the second reading of Bill No. 365, to amend the Regulations Act.
Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North
Centre):	Mr. Speaker, as I indicated when
this bill was given first reading, and as I started out to indicate on Tuesday of this week, the purpose of this bill is to abolish the right which the government now has to pass secret orders in council. I think it should be made clear again that this right to withhold orders in council from publication, although it has been used in relation to an order in council passed under the Emergency Powers Act, is to be found in the Regulations Act. The Regulations Act was enacted in 1950 and it includes section 9, subsection 2, which reads as follows:
The governor In council may by regulation exempt any regulation or class of regulations from the operation of section three, section four, subsection one of section six, and section seven, but every regulation made under this subsection shall be published in English and in French in the Canada Gazette within thirty days after it is made and shall be laid before parliament within fifteen days after it is published in the Canada Gazette or, if parliament is not then in session, within fifteen days after the commencement of the next ensuing session thereof.
The effect of that subsection is that if the governor in council has passed an order in council which it desires to withhold from publication or in other words which it desires to keep secret, it carries out that wish to keep that order in council secret by passing another regulation exempting the previous order in council from publication. That exempting regulation has to be made public, but all it contains is the number and the date of the order in council which has been kept secret.
There is one other reference in the Regulations Act by way of a cross-reference to section 9, subsection 2, which would have to be dealt with in any bill seeking to abolish this right; but the main requirement, in order to get rid of the right to pass secret orders

in council, is that section 9, subsection 2, of the Regulations Act be repealed.
When this matter was before parliament in 1950 there was very little discussion on it. There were a few questions when the Prime Minister was putting the bill through on June 12, 1950, but in the main it would be only fair to say that the house did not realize the full import of that legislation, and let it go through giving the government the right to withhold orders in council from publication. As I say, that right is in the Regulations Act; therefore it refers to orders in council passed under any other statute that is in operation.
There is only one order in council which has been kept secret. It is the one passed on July 4, 1951, under the provisions of the Emergency Powers Act. But it would be possible under section 9, subsection 2, of the Regulations Act for an order in council passed under any other statute to be kept secret. For example, suppose there was a report under the combines act which the government desired to keep secret. At the present time the Combines Investigation Act requires the publishing of reports under that act within a certain time limit. But if it is possible under the Combines Investigation Act to pass an order in council that a certain report does not need to be published, then that order in council could, by virtue of section 9, subsection 2, of the Regulations Act, be kept secret. Therefore we could have the performance repeated that we had in 1949 of a document like the flour milling report being kept secret, only this time it could be regularized because of this right to pass secret orders in council.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that parliament made a mistake in 1950 when it passed this provision, and I think parliament's view that it was a mistake has been demonstrated by the opposition to secret orders in council which has been voiced in this parliament on many occasions since that time. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that parliament should now withdraw the right it gave to the government in 1950 to keep orders in council secret.
There are many other aspects of order in council government which we do not like and against which we register protests from time to time. We had an instance not so long ago when the Emergency Powers Act was used to pass an order in council despite the fact that parliament was right here in session. Our views on that matter were expressed. This does not deal with that. We voted against the extension of the Emergency Powers Act, but we were beaten on that.
68108-317J
Regulations Act
This question as to whether or not the government should still have the right to keep orders in council secret has not been before us yet this session. In fact it has not been before us since it was enacted in 1950. In my view the least this parliament should do before the end of this session is to pass this measure and take away this right to keep orders in council secret.
If parliament is to do that, there is one little problem that faces us, namely the question of the one secret order in council that is now in existence, the one which was passed on July 4, 1951. It seems to me that parliament is in no position to decide whether or not that was a proper subject for a secret order in council, because we know nothing about it. That being the case, it appears that parliament would simply have to take the position that any bill such as mine should not affect any order in council or any regulation now in effect. My bill does that by two sections, section 3 and section 6, which provide that nothing in this bill shall affect any regulation made before the coming into force of this act. In other words, this bill would be in effect from now on.
I do not wish what I have just said to be interpreted as being any approval on my behalf of secret orders in council at any time, not even the one that is in existence. But since we do not know the facts about that one we cannot pass judgment upon it. But it does seem to me that the whole principle of secret orders in council, particularly in peacetime, is completely contrary to democratic processes, and that parliament should give effect to its opposition to this practice by passing this bill before this session ends.
I should like to speak longer, but in view of the limited time that is left for private members' bills obviously I had better not take any longer. The bill itself is drafted in what might appear to be a complicated manner because of the cross-references in the Regulations Act itself. But the main section of Bill No. 365, which is now before the house, is section 2 which reads:
Subsection (2) of section 9 of the said act is repealed.
In other words, that would remove from the Regulations Act the right to keep orders in council secret, and I believe that it is the sense of this House' of Commons. I think we have had evidence that there is some concern about this order in council business even on the government side of the house, and I think it is the sense of this House of Commons that it is a job that we should do before this session ends. As we go into the

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Regulations Act
period of a general election we should not leave this government, of all governments, with the right not only to govern by order in council, but to pass secret orders in council. Therefore I urge the house to support this bill.

maintopic: REGULATIONS ACT
subtopic: REPEAL OP SECRECY PROVISION RESPECTING ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I should like to say just a very few words in support of this measure. We had extensive discussions at an earlier stage of the session with regard to order in council government, and I believe the time has long since passed when this power to legislate by secret orders in council should be done away with. They are entirely contrary to the whole Canadian background, in fact to the background of any truly democratic country, and they smack altogether too much of dictatorship.
Here we have the opportunity for a government to pass an order in council which orders Canadians to do or to refrain from doing some act. Then that order in council can be declared to be secret by means of passing a second order in council, and the people have no way whatever of knowing what the law is and whether or not they are contravening any law. It is fundamental that people in Canada must be able to find out what the laws are. As a matter of fact, the great majority of the people should be behind the laws if they are to be effective. How can that possibly be done when the law is made by an order in council which is kept secret?
I am firmly convinced that this power is just a case of the government being spoiled by the powers it had during the war. It is another example of a power-mad government. I quite agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that the time has come when this power should be taken away from this government and any future government.

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: REGULATIONS ACT
subtopic: REPEAL OP SECRECY PROVISION RESPECTING ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
One cannot help but feel that the hon. gentleman who introduced this bill has misconceived the whole purpose of the sections of the Regulations Act which he is proposing to amend. He seems to think of them entirely in terms of what he refers to as secret orders in council. But I am sure if he will cast his mind back to the time when the Regulations Act was introduced in May, 1950, he will recall that before that time there had been a good deal of urging-I will not say agitation-upon the part of members of the opposition for an amendment by which the large mass of federal legislative orders in council might be published in the Canada Gazette in an orderly manner, in a manner

which would enable the citizens affected by them to refer to the Gazette in about as convenient a way as they would refer to the statutes of Canada, in order to see how they would be affected by these legislative orders in council.
The hon. member will recall that on that occasion the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) reviewed the arrangements which had preceded the Regulations Act which, as he pointed out were, in one sense, of a rather experimental character, in that we were attempting to find at that stage how these arrangements would work, before we introduced a bill to have the procedure enacted by statute. The Prime Minister at that time, after reviewing the previous arrangements at some length, said as reported at page 3040 of Hansard for May 31, 1950:
We feel that the time has now come when we can bring to parliament something that should be practical and workable, and which may not have to be varied too frequently or too soon. This does provide unequivocally for the compulsory publication and tabling of all instruments made under the delegated legislative powers; that is the sole purpose of this measure. Although largely based on the statutory orders and regulations order, 1947, this bill will further clarify and extend the procedure, in order to ensure that it covers the whole field of delegated legislation.
Now, what was the central idea?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: REGULATIONS ACT
subtopic: REPEAL OP SECRECY PROVISION RESPECTING ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: I think the minister will agree that that statement was qualified by the Prime Minister later in that same session.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: REGULATIONS ACT
subtopic: REPEAL OP SECRECY PROVISION RESPECTING ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I shall come to that. I shall cover the point my hon. friend has in mind.
What was the central idea of this measure? It was, as I apprehend it, to make provision for the publication in the Canada Gazette of all of those legislative orders in council which were of general public interest, and at the same time provide, as it does provide, that the Canada Gazette, for the purposes of those who wished to refer to it to find out what these legislation orders in council in the general public interest were, would not be cluttered up with a lot of other orders in council which either were not of general interest, or the publication of which was provided for by some other means such, for example, as under the Canada Grain Act, where the department is required, under the terms of its own statute, to publish all orders that are in force every year, and distribute them among those people who might have an interest in the operations of the Canada Grain Act.
The purpose of this Regulations Act was also that the Canada Gazette would not be cluttered up with orders passed under the Department of Defence Production Act which would be addressed, we will say, to a single manufacturer in respect of a single order or

contract he was carrying out directing him to do such and such a thing within a certain period of time.
To that end it was provided in the section my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre now wishes to amend, namely section 9 (2) that-
The governor in council may by regulation exempt-
And I would ask hon. members to follow these words.
-any regulation or class of regulations from the operation of section three, section four, subsection one of section six, and section seven, but every regulation made under this subsection shall be published in English and in French in the Canada Gazette within thirty days after it is made and shall be laid before parliament within fifteen days after it is published in the Canada Gazette or, if parliament is not then in session, within fifteen days after the commencement of the next ensuing session thereof.
To listen to the hon. member's remarks this afternoon one would think that the only order in council to which section 9(2) refers is this secret order in council. Actually it has a very wide reference to a very large number of other classes of orders in council.
I can remember that at the time the drafting of this measure was being undertaken in the Department of Justice, there was a very extensive examination of the procedure followed in other countries, in order to achieve the purpose of the legislation, which was to provide in a compendious form in the Canada, Gazette, for the public of Canada, all of the orders in council of a legislative nature, by themselves, and that they should not be cluttered up with administrative orders, routine orders, and orders which are of a special interest, let us say, to the grain trade and the like.
We, as we thought, went to an enormous amount of trouble to try to produce in the statute	a means	by	which	the	objective,which I have just stated, could be achieved in a way that was accommodating to the citizen who wished to know what the order in council	now was,	in	order	that	he mightobserve	it; and also	in a	way	in whichthose who might be charged with a breach of the	order in	council could,	when so
charged, be protected adequately in their defence.
Therefore it was provided in section 6 (3)- and this is one of the other sections with which my hon. friend is dealing-that:
(3) No regulation is invalid by reason only that it was not published in the Canada Gazette, but no person shall be convicted for an offence consisting of a contravention of any regulation that was not published in the Canada Gazette unless-
And this covers the point made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra.
Regulations Act
(a)	the regulation was, pursuant to section nine, exempted from the operation of subsection one, or the regulation expressly provides that it shall operate according to its terms prior to publication in the Canada Gazette, and
(b)	it is proved that at the date of the alleged contravention reasonable steps had been taken for the purpose of bringing the purport of the regulation to the notice of the public, or the persons likely to be affected by it, or of the person charged.
So no person in Canada could be convicted under any of these orders in council which had not been published unless it was proved that at the date of an alleged contravention the purport of the order in council had reasonably been brought to his attention.
Now, the Regulations Act contemplated that, in relation for example to an order made under the Department of Defence Production Act and served on a manufacturer to the effect, say, that his work was to be stepped up within 30 days, no one else would be interested. The service of the order would be the publication, so far as the manufacturer was concerned; and nobody else would be interested in the order. And it would not be in the manufacturer's interests at all that this order, addressed to him, should be published perhaps for the benefit of all his competitors.

Mr. Chairman, item 266 is the annual vote for health insurance studies. Associated with it is the provision for the

Supply-Health and Welfare administration of the general health grants. I shall reserve any further remarks that I have to make on the health grants until we get to item 267 where they can, I think, be just as appropriately made.
Right now I would like to say a few words about the first part of item 266, namely health insurance studies. The first question on my mind is this: How long do these studies have to be carried on before we get action on health insurance? Another speaker here this afternoon expressed the fact that there was some confusion in his mind about what health insurance is. I am sure there is no confusion in the mind of the minister or in the minds of those who are working on this question in his department. He and they know that for many years it has been said that the aim of the government, the aim of the Liberal party, is eventually to establish health insurance in Canada.
Mr. King in May, 1948, when he first announced the health grants program, said that one of its purposes was to lay the foundation for health insurance. When some of us have asked for health insurance, namely for a financial arrangement to enable people to pay for hospital and medical care, the reply on some occasions has been that there is no use having a health insurance program until there are sufficient facilities, until hospitals are built and so on. There is no point, say the opponents of health insurance, in enabling people to demand and pay for health care unless that care is there for them.
Well, that argument may have had some validity in 1948-1 do not think it had even then-but certainly it has far less validity now in view of the government's own claim to have made so much headway in connection with the building of hospitals. As a matter of fact, a week ago today the minister boasted of the fact that the target for hospital beds set in 1948 had been surpassed. Well, as I say, Mr. Chairman, it is the clear understanding of those in the department that health insurance is the aim of the health grants program. The aim of that program is to establish sufficient facilities so that it will then be possible to provide health insurance, to make it possible for the people to procure the services that are available.	_	_
I indicated this afternoon that this is spelled out in the last available report of the Department of National Health and Welfare, the report for the year ending March 31, 1952. On page 13 we are given half a page about the purposes of the national health program. Those purposes are listed as four basic aims, and the fourth and last of the basic aims is: "to lay sound foundations for health insurance".
tMr. Knowles.]
Now, under this item of health insurance studies the matter has been studied across the years. The benefits of those studies, to some extent at any rate, have been made available to members of parliament in a number of documents giving the results of research on health insurance plans of other countries. Meanwhile, work on tabulation of the sickness survey and of the provincial health survey reports is expected to provide extremely valuable information-

speechtext: You have my word too, so far as it goes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
-as a result of the co-operative efforts of the federal and provincial governments is an effort that must not be passed by as insignificant, because it is of the greatest significance. Everyone knows where I stand on these matters, but I say this. The most dishonest thing that can be done in this particular field-in the absence of the preparatory stages, including the building of hospitals, providing the personnel required and so on-would be to impose a hurried and incomplete system of this kind. It would both defeat the purposes and not be really in keeping with responsible government.
This country is committed now to a great expenditure for the prosecution of the defence of the freedom of the civilized world. If I were to introduce a proposal now which would cost this country an additional $600 million, I should like to know what the judgment of the people of Canada would be. I think most people in Canada who give this matter careful thought recognize that this is a problem that must be approached as an objective if ultimately it is going to be soundly dealt with. It may be slow. We

may be cautious. But it is better to consolidate our gains as we go along than ultimately have an objective which we have suddenly created and which is impossible to maintain. I for one would not make such a proposal to this parliament or to my colleagues in the government. That stand I think will commend itself to most people in Canada.
Another thing my hon. friend always fails to mention is that this is a responsibility in a federal state that cannot be discharged only by the central government. When this program was announced, the federal government provided funds to all the provinces to make a survey of their needs in terms of health standards and health facilities. Each of the provinces has made this survey and they are monumental documents, generally speaking. I do not know whether or not those documents have been carefully examined but as Minister of National Health and Welfare I would certainly have to put before parliament and before my colleagues the recommendations contained in the ten provincial surveys in respect of this particular matter; and that I would do.
My hon. friend-with the best of intentions, I know

talks about these matters. If he' sat where I sit, he would want to know what the cost would be. There is no one in this chamber tonight and there is no one in this country today who could tell me what that cost is. I hope that very soon after the assessment has been made of the national sickness survey that is now being tabulated we shall have a good idea. When we have that, we shall then be able to give this matter further consideration.
Some hon. gentlemen say that I brought in this program last week for election purposes. I think that is fair comment; but it is not correct comment. I will not say there are no occasions when, like every other hon. member, I am guided by political interest. But I will say this. I have given my best over the five years of this program. I am sure my hon. friend, with the chivalry which I know he possesses, would be the first to say

if he does not find it against political interest- that this national health program of ours has been pursued as has perhaps no other program, and with less political purpose in mind.
I have given credit to the provinces at every interval. I must say that they in turn have given credit to us. Only in today's morning paper we have a statement of the minister of health in Ontario. I shall not repeat what he said because he makes a personal reference, but I will say that in

addition to the personal reference he spoke of the co-operative consideration of this government; and that is also true of the minister of health in Saskatchewan. One has to note the words of the premier of Quebec, only last Saturday, when he referred to the help this program meant to the province of Quebec.
My hon. friend talks about health insurance as though it were sickness insurance. We have health insurance now, at this very time, and in a concrete way. My hon. friend shakes his head. Let him examine what we have done in the field of public health. Let him see what we have done in the field of tuberculosis- control. Let him look at what we have done to counter crippling conditions in children. Let him look at what we have done to try to direct cancer control in this country. Let him look and see what we have done in the field of mental health, in hospital construction, in medical and scientific research and in professional training. Those are all necessary conditions. To use the language of Sir Stanford Cade, one of the outstanding authorities in his field in the world, we have embarked upon a responsible system, taking into account our financial opportunities and our over-all obligations, and taking into account the basic context of the constitution of this country.
I know my hon. friend will agree with me when he thinks of what the situation was in this country seven years ago and compares it with the situation today. As a result of the co-operation we have had between the two senior levels of government in the pursuit of the objective which I think all of us in all parties have in mind, I would have hoped he might say that we have made a significant start in the realization of that objective.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are just three things I want to say. First of all, the minister knows that I was amongst those in this chamber in May, 1948, who applauded wholeheartedly and generously when the then prime minister announced the health grants program and that we in this party across the years have welcomed and appreciated everything that has been done under the health grants program. We welcomed the extension of that program announced by the minister last Friday night.
But, Mr. Chairman, that does not deny to us or to the people of Canada the right to point out that a health grants program is not health insurance, and that we are asking for that further step which this government and the Liberal party have been promising
Supply-Health and Welfare across the years. I continue to applaud and to appreciate the health grants program, but it has not paid a single Canadian's hospital bill. It has not removed the burden of the cost of illness from the shoulders of a single Canadian family. Until we take that further step, the program is not complete by any manner of means.
The next thing I want to say is this, Mr. Chairman. I am startled at the minister standing up tonight and saying that these grants, these facilities and these services that are being provided are health insurance. He knows that health insurance involves a fund to enable people to pay for hospital and medical care. He knows that his own departmental report still says that the aim of the program is to lay sound foundations for health insurance. He has said that himself time and time again. He has said that health insurance-he said it tonight-has to wait until we have the facilities and, in his language, until we can meet the cost.
My friend the hon. member for Saskatoon is pointing out, as we have pointed out time and time again, that this is one case where the law of supply and demand might be put to work. If you had in the pockets of the people more of the money to pay for health services through a health insurance fund, that demand would in itself help to increase the facilities that are available.
There is just one other comment I wish to make at this time, and it is in the form of a question which I put directly to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In view of his statement tonight, and in view of the clear indication that, so far as he is concerned, he does not envisage the inauguration of a health insurance program at the present time, will he make sure that the Liberal party, in the next election, refrains from promising to the people of Canada health insurance which it is now clear the Liberals do not intend to bring in?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Shall this item carry?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was not intending to say anything on this item, but I heard the minister make his speech and for once in my life I must congratulate him for giving an excellent speech. I am going to suggest that it was one of the best antisocialist speeches I have heard him give in this chamber. He did it with vigour. He watched his words. It was a sensible speech, and my only hope is that it came from his heart and not his head. I want him to analyse his words. His plea was right. How can you go to the people of Canada today, with vast expenditures on defence, and ask them for

Supply-Health and Welfare another $600 million, as he says? You cannot do it. What I want to ask the minister is: When there is no defence expenditure, is he going to appeal then to his head and say: I am going to the people now and ask them for another $600 million? I hope at that time he will have a heart.
I am saying that I am not against a certain type of health insurance. I would rather use the word "assurance" than "insurance". I believe that we have to assure the people of Canada health and welfare, but I do not believe we must do it by imposing upon them economic slavery.
We hear a lot today about an over-all health insurance scheme. We have letters come to our desks; we have petitions presented to us; we have organizations, and some very prominent and large ones, come to us and present their views. But I am always tempted-perhaps I should not yield to the temptation; perhaps I should try to sing that old hymn: "Yield not to temptation, for yielding is sin"-to say: I wonder whether these views express the intelligent views of the rank and file of the people of Canada. I am tempted to ask that every time.
If the minister and his department should carry on any research in respect to health insurance, there is one little bit of research I wish he would carry on, and that is an attempt to learn the wish of the rank and file of the people of Canada. He has told us, for instance, that to embark on such a scheme would cost about $600 million. How does that figure out in taxes in this country of 14 million people? Well, it figures out at approximately $50 a person. Here is a man and his wife and two children, we will say, a moderate family. If it figures out at $200 a year when you investigate and carry on your research, I wonder what would happen if you placed a plebiscite before the people and not merely asked them "Are you in favour of an over-all health insurance plan," but laid all the cards on the table face up and asked this question: "Are you desirous of an over-all health insurance plan which is going to increase your taxes $50 a year for every person in your family?" I wonder what sort of a vote you would get on a national plebiscite of that kind. That is something to consider.
In my views I suppose I am a bit of a traditionalist. I suppose I am conservative in my views, not politically conservative; but I am not always ready to accept every sort of highfalutin scheme that may sound good and be pictured as a good thing. I am pretty steady when it comes to accepting new things. I think modern art is the art of crazy men; modern architecture is the

architecture of people who have no vision, or no appreciation of beauty, but I am not talking about that.
I see your eyes are fastened on me, Mr. Chairman, but I am not ready to accept all sorts of new schemes. I say we need to find out exactly what the people themselves want. The people do want health; they do want services. What they want most is an income that will guarantee that they can have those services and pay for them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
It is not my intention to enter into any debate at the present time. I did not expect any debate on health insurance. Perhaps the minister was absent on the last occasion, namely the first week in December when this matter was fully discussed in the house and an amendment was moved by the leader of the C.C.F. party, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. At that time I placed the feeling and policy of this party on the record, as I think every other party in the house did, and we have not departed from that up to the present time. That still stands as our party policy.
To get back to the item, I am interested to know where this money is being spent. I note that there is a director of health insurance studies, two medical officers, an executive officer, and then a certain number of clerks and stenographers which would be necessary. Then we come down to the items of travelling expenses, freight, express and cartage and educational and other informational publications. Then there is a large item of $12,000. What form do the educational and other informational publications take? The minister has assured us in his speech that at no place is there anything political. Can he assure us that at no place in this educational program going out from the department in the form of papers is there anything political? What is the form that these educational papers take?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The explanation of the $12,000 increase is the information obtained in Canada's sickness survey, $11,000; then the report on the operation of the health grants program for the provinces in the five years, costing $1,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I have just one question. Have all the provinces sent in the results of their studies?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: All but Newfoundland; it is in the course of preparation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Does the minister know how the study is in regard to Newfoundland, whether it will be received soon?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes, very shortly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I would feel that I was remiss in my duty if I did not say a few words on

the estimates of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. If you will look at the record, Mr. Chairman, you will find that I have not said anything so far on his estimates.
On this whole question of health, health grants and health insurance I give credit largely to the Minister of National Health and Welfare for what has been done since the establishment of the department. He is the first minister, and there is no doubt that we have made more progress in that field since the department was established and placed under his guidance than we made in the previous 50 years, at least.
I agree with him that the steps the department is taking in establishing these provincial grants are necessary to the development of an over-all health program. I should like to bring to the minister's attention this fact. These health grants for the purpose of providing more bed space in the different provinces must be matched dollar for dollar by provincial grants. The province has to put up dollar for dollar.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Just in some grants.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It does in the building of hospitals, for example.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: In the hospital construction grant, in the cancer control grant, in the venereal disease grant at their request, and in the rehabilitation grant-it is only in those.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
With grants made in that way it is not possible to have uniform development across the country, for the simple reason that the provincial incomes of British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario and, perhaps, Quebec, enable them to take full advantage of the grants made by the federal government. In that way they are in a position to build faster and to provide more bed space.
I just mention this to point up the fact that the provinces with the low provincial incomes, and with very little chance of increasing those incomes, are going to lag behind for some considerable time unless there is a more equitable distribution based upon the ability of the provinces to take advantage of the grants.
Second-and this was what I had chiefly in mind when I rose to speak-I must say I cannot understand the attitude indicated this afternoon by the hon. member for Peace River, and again tonight by the hon. member for Macleod; because the record indicates, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Lanark, that this group moved an amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne in which we asked for the development of a national health program. When that vote was taken both the hon. member for Macleod and the hon. member for Peace
Supply-Health and Welfare River, with the other members of that group in the house, voted for the amendment.
I wish to straighten out the record on this point, because only a moment ago the hon. member for Macleod suggested that a plebiscite of the rank and file should be taken on this question. Well, if the hon. member for Macleod cannot remember what he did in December of last year, if he does not know exactly what he voted for, so far as the introduction of a national health program is concerned, then surely it is not possible to go out into the country and take a plebiscite recording the opinion of the man in the street, who has had very little opportunity of discussing or understanding these problems. Surely it would be unwise to do that, when hon. members in the House of Commons are inconsistent enough to reverse their opinions and indicate a complete misunderstanding of what they are talking about, particularly after they have voted on a subject that was thoroughly debated in the house only a couple of months ago.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Of course that is not true.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The record shows it; I just took a look at it.	'

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It does not show any such thing.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Read our statements.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I certainly would vote the way I talked. You are admitting now that you double-talked when you voted the other way -and for what reason I do not know.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: You are all mixed up.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I do not want to get into a prolonged debate on that, because when the amendment was moved I made a statement; and if the hon. member for Peace River is interested he may read it. This afternoon he asked someone to spell out exactly what we have in mind when we make reference to a national health program. Well, if he will look at Hansard for December 9, 1952 he will find that at page 493 I have spelled out the mechanics of a national health program. If he will read it he will have some idea of what we have in mind when we refer to a national health program.
I believe that such a program in this country is a must. The minister is right when he says the department has made a good deal of progress through health grants. But if anyone wanted to be frank about the subject he would have to admit that the facilities for the health of the people of this country have never been worse than they are today. Costs have gone up tremendously. And let no one forget that we are bringing in about 150,000 people each year through immigration,

Supply-Health and Welfare and that we have been doing this for the past five or six years. We are setting them down in organized centres where medical facilities have to be provided.
Take a look at any section of this country today and you will find that it is more difficult for the average person to get into a hospital and obtain medical treatment than ever before in the history of this country. You do not even have to leave this city of Ottawa to find that condition. Anyone who is interested need only take a look at the availability of doctors and dentists in this city, and the possibility of being admitted to a hospital, to have a clear understanding of what I mean. And that situation obtains right straight across the country.
Cost is a big factor. The Minister of Finance has indicated that there are 137,000 families in Canada who receive incomes below taxation level. Their incomes are not high enough to be assessed for tax. That being so, and in the light of today's costs of medical services, one can be assured that at least that group of people are not in a position from a financial standpoint to provide any kind of medical service for themselves.
In some of the low-income provinces it will be years before the people will be able to take advantage of the opportunities afforded today. Saskatchewan has a quite satisfactory hospital insurance system. It is working well. I agree with the hon. member who says that unless a scheme is established there will be no development of the mechanics, but that when the scheme is there the other things will follow rapidly. In Saskatchewan an extra tax of $10 per individual gives complete hospital coverage, with a $30 maximum per family. I know claims have been paid under the Saskatchewan scheme running from $7,000 to $10,000. Where would the average individual be if he were confronted with medical bills of that kind? The rest of his life would be mortgaged.
In British Columbia a type of hospital insurance is in use, and has been found most helpful. My information indicates that ward treatment can be obtained for about $3.50 a day whereas, without such a scheme, it would cost anywhere from $8 to $16. Then there is another type of insurance in Ontario. But in the other provinces we do not have that sort of thing; so in most provinces we are committed provincially to the acceptability of health insurance. This type of insurance is provided in the army, the navy and the air force. These services give complete coverage, with the best of equipment and the best of doctors. The same has been established in veterans' hospitals right across the country.
[Mr. Glllis.l
Most people who sneer at socialized medicine do not know what it means. They are content to repeat a slogan developed in Wall street, New York, without having the slightest idea of what it is all about. The veterans have complete coverage; yet we do not describe it as socialized medicine. We call it a service they earned, and the country has been big enough to provide the best for them. All through the armed services there is complete coverage. But the person who digs and works and pays the taxes which provide all these things has no protection when he hits a period of sickness. That is his position if he is in that 137,000 indicated by the Minister of Finance who pay their share toward the wealth of the country and make these services available to others.
We are told that we cannot afford it, but let us take a look at the question of cost for one minute. The statement was made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare that this country is paying about $600 million a year in medical services of one kind or another. In my opinion a good deal of that is wasted through maladministration and duplication. If the federal government through the federal health department would establish a system of national health insurance and rechannel that money now being spent by various organizations and individuals, there would be little additional cost involved. That is the way it would be done. It is a lot of nonsense to talk about more taxes, and the person who makes that statement is not thinking the matter through.
I agree with the minister that if I were sitting in his place I would want to know where the money was coming from, but I am reasonably sure that there are in the department today men who have the facts and figures of where that $600 million a year is going, and also those who can tell him how to rechannel that money through the services under his department in a way that would entail very little additional cost.
We are beginning to see a little daylight in connection with defence expenditures. I think the time has come when the federal government should indicate that they believe in a national health program and will establish it as soon as possible. Do not forget for one minute that in 1945 the prime minister made proposals to the provinces. He was not afraid of it. He made the definite proposal to the provinces that he would establish a national health program that was going to cost the federal government some $480 million. All he wanted the provinces to do was agree.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: $200 million, but it was contingent upon tax agreements being signed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: He wanted the co-operation of the provinces to carry out the administration and mechanics. Nine provinces agreed, and I think one more would be willing to agree at this time. The province of Ontario, which was largely instrumental in upsetting the dominion-provincial agreements in 1945, has established a provincial scheme of its own. Although it is quite inadequate at the present time it does indicate that they have accepted the principle. I understand that Ontario has also signed a dominion tax agreement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: They are wise.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The hon. member has not been here enough to understand the mechanics of these things. You could get an agreement from the other province. If the prime minister in his wisdom felt in 1945 that we could do it, I am sure it is just as reasonable to think that we can do it today. The question of cost seems to be the big thing. Everyone who does not want to do anything and has not thought the thing through very far gets up immediately and says, "Are you going to tax the Canadian people some more?"
My experience is that the Canadian people are quite willing to pay taxes for anything from which they receive a benefit. You never hear anyone making much of a squawk about the 2 per cent social security tax. They accepted that and lauded it because it was for the benefit of people and in recognition of past services. It is an aid to people, to help them through their later years of life.
Go into any community from Vancouver to Prince Edward Island and you will find, despite what the hon. member for Macleod has said, that most people are asking, "Where are we going to get protection against hospital and doctor bills which may mortgage us for the rest of our lives?" That is the thing that is uppermost in their minds. Let me tell the minister of health and welfare that if he wants to be political in this next election, if he wants to get a lot of votes, this is the issue that should be settled.
In only two weeks we obtained over 100,000 signatures on a petition which was sent in here to the House of Commons. If we had had six weeks in which to circulate that petition across the country we would have got half the people to sign. It was done quickly, but it settled all doubts as to where the people stand. I tell you that when I am home in my community, and I think this applies generally to all hon. members, I find I am bothered most by men and women coming in and asking how they can get in hospitals without paying the admission fee. They
Supply-Health and Welfare are concerned about the cost of hospitalization. They want to know how they can get a doctor. That is what you hear morning, noon and night.
I know there is no doubt in the minister's mind. I know the minister is quite willing and he is going as far as the treasury board and perhaps others in the government will permit him to go.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: My hon. friend has been talking about hospitalization. Does he realize that under our program we have assisted in providing 2,400 additional beds in his own province?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I realize that fully. I point out to the minister that while he has provided these extra beds he has not provided the means by which a large percentage of the population can get' into those hospital beds. The minister's department has helped to establish a wonderful institution in Halifax in the Victoria general hospital. It is second to none in Canada from the standpoint of equipment, service and staff. But there are thousands of people in Nova Scotia who need treatment which could be given by that centre but who cannot afford to go there. I contend that we should provide means to enable these people to take advantage of the facilities that we have established.
I am not going to say a great deal more on this matter, but I did think it was my duty to say something in the light of the statements made this afternoon by the hon. member for Peace River and this evening by the hon. member for Macleod. I think their memories required a little jogging on how they voted just a few weeks ago.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: May I inform the committee that some of our colleagues have to attend the meeting of the standing committee on agriculture. Some of them desire to say a word on the next item and perhaps we could permit them to take the floor now and speak on this item. The next item has to do with health grants and this one has to do with the administration of general health grants.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I thank the committee for its kindness in allowing me to say a few words at this time. I have taken up the matter I have in mind with the minister before, and for that reason I shall not take a great deal of time to say what I want to say.
I want to urge the minister to make a larger grant to the West Kildonan health clinic. We have had considerable correspondence on this matter, and I have also spoken to the minister about it. I ask him to give further consideration to granting
5024	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare them more assistance. They are only able to have clinics twice a week, and there are a lot of the children there who still have to have their teeth examined. If we could get enough money to allow them to have three clinics a week I think we could catch up on the backlog.
The other thing I want to ask the minister about, or remind him about again, is this. We have about 800 retarded children of school age in Manitoba, and those children cannot go to school. I understand that it is a criminal offence to send them to school, but they could get a certain amount of education in a special school that might fit them in some kind of a way to perhaps make a living, or be some help to their parents. An organization has been founded there recently, and I shall just quote a little bit from their brief and let it go at that. Before I do so I will say that I know this is something the federal government could not do alone. They would have to have the co-operation of the province. With a sympathetic minister here at Ottawa, and I know that the people in Manitoba are good fellows, I think we would be able to do something for these 800 retarded children in Manitoba.
The petition reads like this:
That we petition the department of education and the department of health to provide day school and special training classes for mentally retarded children who are living at home by:
Extending the public school act to provide that in any school district where there are at least fifteen children of school age who are mentally retarded, but who are deemed by the provincial psychiatrist to be capable of benefiting from special instruction, it shall be compulsory for that district to provide the special instruction required.
Exploring terms of the health education and mental health grants now provided by the department of national health at Ottawa through the provincial department of health to see if some of these moneys can be spent to provide the supplementary grants required for such classes and to provide intelligence testing services so that there is proper screening of children for these classes and to pay scholarships to Manitoba teachers to take special training for this work.
I have met school teachers who have specialized in this, and I think there is a future for it. I would ask the minister to give consideration to these two items. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Kootenay West has also an appointment and wishes to speak now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
My subject comes under the next item. Thank you for your kind consideration, Mr. Chairman. I wish to speak very briefly with respect to the hospital question. I listened to the minister very carefully when he made his opening remarks, and I was interested in the great gains that had
[Mr. Bryce.1

been made in the number of hospital beds; but as far as the district I represent is concerned the need for hospital extension and new hospitals and more beds is still very urgent, as it is in many other places. I know, Mr. Chairman, that it is a very urgent problem which is faced by several communities I represent, owing to old hospitals becoming obsolete, the high cost of building new ones, the increasing population, and so on. I know this question has been of very serious concern particularly to the communities of Nelson and Castlegar. For some three or four years they have been almost up against a blank wall. They cannot afford to build a new hospital and they cannot afford to build extensions.
While the present grants are very helpful I think under the present circumstances they are not sufficient. I was interested to note that the minister said the savings made in grants for hospitals could be used for other purposes, and I thought the purposes were excellent. However, I have been asked by various hospital boards in my constituency to bring to the minister's attention the fact that there is a very pressing problem in that the $1,000 grant for a hospital bed and $1,500 for a chronic bed is quite insufficient. They ask that he give consideration to their particular problems and their need for larger grants. I have met the members of the boards in question and they are hard-working people who give their time voluntarily, trying to solve their problems on a local basis. I have discussed their problems with them on many occasions and I know this is a matter of very great concern to them.
I just speak briefly because I do not want to take much time at this stage of the estimates, but I told them that I would mention it.

I think these people who are worried about national health insurance had better ask that the item we are discussing now be deleted or reduced to $1, because the item is headed "health insurance studies". If that means anything, to me it means it is the forerunner of national health insurance. I am not going to cover that field. Like the hon. member for Lanark, I feel that we had our day on it when we were discussing it on the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
At that time we were accused by some speakers of not taking any notice of the reports that were made in connection with the health studies in the provinces. I am going to draw the attention of the committee to the report from the province of British Columbia, and the recommendations contained in it. The recommendations are brief, so I shall not prolong what I have to say by elaborating on them. I am quoting from "Survey of health services and facilities in British Columbia, in existence on December 31, 1948." A note attached to the cover of the copy sent to me has this wording on it:
This copy of the British Columbia health survey report, "Survey of health services and facilities in British Columbia, 1948" is being sent to you with the compliments of the health branch, department of health and welfare, Victoria, B.C.
Then under that is the name "G. R. F. Elliott, M.D., C.M., D.P.H., assistant provincial health officer." This is quite a lengthy study, and there are parts of it that I should like
5026	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare to quote but I am not going to take the time of the committee to do so. After asserting that the principle of health insurance was sound, the report states:
It is felt, however, that certain general recommendations can be made which will allow further progress to be made toward comprehensive medical care with no financial barrier, which, although likely inevitable, must be approached with much study and care.
It is therefore recommended:
(1)	That comprehensive health insurance be not introduced at present, but receive further study:
(2)	That consideration be given to the introduction of plans which would cover some medical services and (or) certain groups of the population (see recommendations in following section) :
(3)	That in any proposed plan of health insurance federal assistance be available through a definite financial formula.
Then they deal with the question of children's health. The report states:
The medical profession today are in an enviable position regarding income, and this fact must be taken into consideration when final costs are established after the necessary consultations and advice have been sought from the medical profession.
It is therefore recommended:
That consideration be given to the introduction of a comprehensive health insurance plan to cover children.
There is nothing ambiguous about that. Then they deal with diagnostic services and the need for them, as well as the difficulties in providing those services. The recommendation is as follows:
It is therefore recommended:
That serious consideration be given to the introduction of a subsidized plan of diagnostic services (laboratory and radiology) and that the centres recognized by the British Columbia hospital insurance service be used for this plan.
They are going rather a long way. Then they deal with the matter of the high cost of drugs, about which we all know. I know about it from personal experience. The report reads:
As pointed out previously, such a system should be inaugurated for any health insurance scheme where government funds are used for the purchase of drugs and allied products. The use of such a system would be compulsory for all individuals for whom drugs are provided completely or partially by government funds. It should be introduced now for any government health insurance scheme in effect, including the social assistance medical service.
It is therefore recommended:
That immediate consideration be given to assuring that wherever government funds are used at present for the purchase of drugs or allied products, these purchases be made direct from the manufacturer.
We are getting rather close to socialization here. There is another recommendation concerning specialized services which reads as follows:
It is therefore recommmended:
That as the need becomes apparent, specialist services, similar to those in effect in such fields as


venereal diseases, tuberculosis, and cancer, be extended to other fields.
Then the last paragraph of the report reads as follows:
This suggested plan for comprehensive health insurance is being presented not as a clear-cut recommendation, but rather as one which has definite possibilities although requiring a good deal of closer study by the government.
It is therefore recommended:
That further close study be given to the medical services association pilot plan entitled "Report on community enrolment."
I would say to those who are -fearful of a national health insurance plan that they had better make for cover, because it is coming.
