speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I believe the churches could do a great deal to relieve the suffering of people for want of hospitals if they would just simply remind the people of Canada that the good Lord said "Six days shall ye work and rest the seventh". During the war we contributed through compulsory savings. Eighty per cent of the people, the recipients of those cheques, when they received them wondered where the money came from. But as long as we are going to keep hollering for shorter hours, more take-home pay, no savings, get it out of the rich or out of those who do save and give it to us for nothing, the worse things are going to be. Then when we cannot make up the required amount, tap the rich; but don't go so deep that you get to the bottom of the barrel. Let us not work seven days a week in this country.

I can give it now if it will save time, but there is another place for it. We have had experiments made in the city of Brantford. To these experiments we have contributed. We have also made studies of the town of Stratford and also of the city of Sarnia. The best view is that the addition of fluorine to water supplies in Canada promises not only to be an important event in the history of preventive dentistry but also one of the most important events in the history of the whole public health field.
Among researchers there is no argument as to whether or not fluorination reduces tooth decay. They all agree that it does so to a marked degree; and they also agree that ill effects, including unsightly mottling of teeth, do not occur. I can only say that the national health department has compared the teeth of children in Brantford, Ontario where the water is fluorinated, with those in Sarnia; and the Brantford children have been found to have 68 per cent less tooth decay. We presume that fact is due to the fluorination of the water supply in Brantford. Similar experiments have been carried out in New Jersey and several other communities in the united States, with similar results.

speechtext:
Under this item 267 it is possible to review briefly the national health program in so far as it affects the province of Ontario. This I propose to do not only because of the deep interest of the citizens of Ontario in the program but because of the interest of Canadians from coast to coast in health.
I can congratulate quite frankly and sincerely the minister upon the action, vigour and imagination which he has shown in the prosecution of the national health program to
5028	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare date. I say he is entitled to great congratulation, because he has been limited by the budgets and the war prevention program of the government. The eyes of Canada are on him. They have been on him in the past and they will be on him in the future, because Canadians hope for better health and a better Canada through better health.
Mr. Chairman, Canadians approve this program and in particular the idea behind the program, namely its objective. The objective of the program is that of the late Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King. He sought for Canadians, in the long-term view, national contributory health insurance. This program leads us there. In other words it leads to making the resources of modern medical skill and modern hospital facilities available to every Canadian citizen, regardless of means, and visualizes a contributory basis. We have made much progress to date. The objective is not yet attained but we are a great deal closer to the objective because of the vigour, the action and the advances of the present minister.
We ask: What of the future? Canadians, and those in Ontario in particular, want more progress. Has there been federal delay? I see no evidence of it. There has been no lack of action on the part of the minister. More than this, grants have been made in excess of what the provinces have been able to implement. We come then to the question of provincial delay, and on that question I say the provinces have been slow, and in particular the province of Ontario is guilty in this respect. Why so? Why the delay? The Korean conflict has not helped. The extraordinary expansion of the economy has been another factor that has hindered the provinces because there have been shortages of material and personnel which have prevented the provinces from doing what they should do in taking up these grants.
The conclusion is obvious. There should be greater use of the grants in Ontario. We hope this use will increase within the immediate foreseeable future.
Why do we turn to the provinces? Not all Canadians understand fully that we have, as the minister stated, a federal system under British parliamentary law. The provinces have the primary responsibility for health. We grant the money and the provinces work out the details.
The benefits of such a system are obvious. In particular we have come to the conclusion in Canada through the long years that if you wish to look after local needs and local traditions in the best possible manner, then you do so by using the federal-provincial


system. But here we are preparing for the objective of the program and seem to become impatient. We can understand this. But remember, other countries have found to their sorrow that there was not enough preparation when they brought their health programs into force in the final phases. We need preparation, and we all agree on that, if we are going to ultimately have a program of complete health services for all, irrespective of means, on a contributory basis.
The preliminary steps are very clear, and the minister is taking them as rapidly as is within his power. We need the physical means of care and we need mobilized personnel such as doctors, dentists, public health workers and similar people to use the facilities. Our shortages at the present are hospital beds and more trained workers.
I turn to Ontario. Here we have the national health program and its grants for hospital construction and health services. Ontario has fallen short of accepting and acting upon the grants which are available under these two heads of hospital construction and health services.
I have a report from the department here in Ottawa which indicates that as of February, 1953, there was available for Ontario $28,119,003 for hospital construction. There was approved $20 million for hospital construction as between the two governments, but at that date there was spent only $11,684,785. Here we have a marked discrepancy between that which was approved and that which was implemented.
I come to the field of health services. Here you have grants to cover such things as crippled children, professional training, venereal disease control, mental health, tuberculosis control, public health and health surveys. Ontario has fallen short of the allocated sums in these fields also. In the fiscal year 1951-52 the allocation for health service grants was $6,541,862; but Ontario took up and accepted merely $3,095,834.
In the light of these figures, Mr. Chairman, I conclude that we aim to see to it that no Canadian need suffer disease or injury which can be prevented, and that Canadians are willing to go ahead with this program and pay the costs. Furthermore, turn your minds to the volqntary health schemes. Those schemes draw many people into them annually and the membership mounts. Canadians are interested in the Blue Cross and similar schemes of that kind. Canadians do want better health standards for all.
We thank the government and the minister for their action at the federal level, and we urge the provinces to do their part on the provincial level, and let us get on with

the implementation of these health service and hospital construction grants.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

I have sat here and
listened to a great deal of talk on these items tonight, and I think a few of us should begin to look at the matter from a practical standpoint. I have listened to people talking about conditions which existed 25 or 30 years ago. Today we are not living in those times. We are not living in days when we take home all we earn, and where we can save a good portion of our salaries. We are now contributing a large part of our income to the national good. The time is long since past when the small community contributed to the welfare of its citizens who, by force of circumstances, through illness or for other reasons, were deprived of their rights.
Today we are living in a time when the cost of living makes possible only a poor existence. For people to stand in this house and talk about looking after themselves in their old age is a lot of balderdash; and it is about time we started to think that way.

I am sorry the hour is so late and that we are so near the end of the session that it is not possible to deal with some matters as fully and as adequately as they should be dealt with. Therefore at this stage of the game I shall abbreviate my remarks with respect to this whole question of social security, which it is proper to discuss under the welfare branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
There are several items here, including family allowances, old age security, old age assistance, blindness allowances and the like. I wish to say as briefly and as forcibly as I can that we still have a long way to go in this country in the field of old age security. I do not wish to detract one iota from the credit due to this 21st parliament for having been the parliament which got rid of the means test in connection with the old age pension, at least for those 70 years of age and over. The minister and others will recall that in 1950, when the special committee on old age security reported its recommendation that that step be taken, together with certain other steps, I indicated that my feeling at that stage was that nothing should be done to jeopardize getting that new plan into operation. But I indicated also that as soon as that plan was in operation I for one would bring to the attention of the government the need for further steps that should be taken.
The fact that we must face is that it is four years since there has been any increase in the amount of the old age pension. It is still only $40 a month. I wish to draw to the attention of the government the urgent need for increasing the amount of the old age pension, both in the 70 years and over bracket where it is known as old age security and is free from the means test and between 65 and 69 years where it is known as old age assistance and up to the present is subject to the means test.
I know that if we get into an argument on this matter we will have the same sort of questions and comments that were raised in respect to that other aspect of social security, a health insurance program, about which we were talking earlier. Bearing in mind your suggestion, Mr. Chairman, that I have given the answers to these questions already, I will content myself with saying that we have dealt with this question of the cost of an adequate old age security time and time again. I will just deal with one aspect of it. At the present time we are devoting about 1 [DOT] 4 per cent of our gross national income to our senior citizens 70 years of age and over who constitute about 5 per cent of our population. I submit that

Supply-Health and Welfare that is not good enough. In my view we should be increasing the old age pension to a figure of not less than $60 per month to make it commensurate with today's cost of living.
Hon. members may moan and groan if they wish, but I am satisfied that we can afford it. Indeed I am satisfied that we cannot afford not to go further in establishing a social security program that is adequate and that measures up to what our people deserve and what our economy can afford. As hon. members know from long experience, I could speak at length on this matter but I shall not do so at this time. I insist that this parliament, in spite of all the credit that is coming to it for what it has done in getting rid of the means test, has not finished the job. I regret very much that it appears that this government is prepared to go to the country this summer without increasing the old age pension to at least $60 per month. Indeed, I feel that the means test should be removed at 65 years, and I hope that even yet these steps will be taken before dissolution. When we get down to the question of blindness allowances I shall have something more to say.
These are not requests for something for nothing; these are not requests along the lines that were expressed a moment ago by an hon. member to my right; they are simply requests for social justice, for recognition of the fact that we live in the kind of world where we work together, where we produce things together and that it is only fair that the people who produce the nation's wealth should get back that wealth in an adequate standard of living during their working years and in proper old age security when the time for retirement comes.
I shall leave it at that for now. I strongly urge an increase in the old age pension in both brackets to not less than $60 a month.
